sections.subtopic: Development of the Periodic Table & the Modern Periodic Law
sections.title: Why chemistry needed a shelving system

board_events.text: Why do we need a Periodic Table?
By the 1800s a new element was appearing every few years - each one memorised from scratch.
The table is a shelving system: it turns that chaos into a map.
The big promise: know WHERE an element sits, and you can predict HOW it behaves.
Even an element nobody has studied is findable - if it behaves like its neighbours, it lives near them.
So position is not decorative: an element's seat encodes its chemistry.
One seat, many predictions
Radius, reactivity, the formula of its oxide - all readable from the place it occupies.

segments.text: <curious>Let me start with a question that bothered every chemist two centuries ago.</curious> Why does chemistry even need a periodic table? What problem was it built to solve?

Picture the eighteen hundreds. A brand new element was being discovered every few years, and for each one its properties had to be learned from scratch. There was no pattern to lean on, no shortcut - just raw memorisation, element by element.

The periodic table is the shelving system that ended that chaos. Think of a giant unorganised store with everything dumped on the floor, and then the same store after a smart shopkeeper racks it: pulses here, spices there. Suddenly everything is findable.
<whisper>Here is the single most powerful promise of the table.</whisper> Once you know where an element sits, you can predict how it behaves - even if nobody has ever studied it.
That is the payoff. An element you have never met becomes predictable, because if it behaves like the things around it, it lives right next to them on the shelf.
So the position of an element is never just decoration. Its seat quietly encodes its chemistry - and that is the whole idea we are going to unpack.
And from that one seat, a surprising amount follows.
Its size, how reactive it is, even the formula of the oxide it forms - all of these can be read straight off the place it occupies. That is the power we are building toward.
<curious>चलो एक सवाल से शुरू करते हैं जो दो सौ साल पहले हर chemist को परेशान करता था।</curious> Chemistry को periodic table की ज़रूरत ही क्यों पड़ी? ये किस problem को solve करने के लिए बना था?

जरा eighteen hundreds को imagine करो। हर कुछ सालों में एक नया element discover हो रहा था, और हर एक की properties scratch से याद करनी पड़ती थीं। कोई pattern नहीं था, कोई shortcut नहीं - बस पूरा rote memorisation, एक-एक element।

Periodic table वही shelving system है जिसने इस chaos को खत्म किया। सोचो एक बड़ा unorganised store जहाँ सब कुछ फर्श पर बिखरा है, और फिर वही store जब एक smart shopkeeper उसे racks में लगा देता है - pulses यहाँ, spices वहाँ। अचानक सब कुछ findable हो जाता है।
अब table का सबसे powerful promise सुनो। एक बार आपको पता चल जाए कि element कहाँ बैठा है, तो आप predict कर सकते हो कि वो कैसे behave करेगा - भले ही किसी ने उसे कभी study न किया हो।
यही तो असली फायदा है। एक element जिससे आप कभी मिले ही नहीं, वो भी predictable बन जाता है, क्योंकि अगर वो अपने आस-पास वालों जैसा behave करता है, तो shelf पर उन्हीं के बगल में बैठता है।
तो element की position कभी सिर्फ सजावट नहीं होती। उसकी seat चुपचाप उसकी chemistry को encode करती है - और यही पूरा idea हम unpack करने वाले हैं।
और उसी एक seat से बहुत कुछ निकल आता है।
<excited>उसका size, कितना reactive है, यहाँ तक कि जो oxide वो बनाता है उसका formula भी - ये सब उसी जगह से पढ़ा जा सकता है जहाँ वो बैठा है।</excited> यही वो power है जिसकी तरफ हम बढ़ रहे हैं।

sections.subtopic: Development of the Periodic Table & the Modern Periodic Law
sections.title: Groups, periods, and the three big leaps

board_events.text: Groups and Periods: reading the map
A vertical column is a GROUP; a horizontal row is a PERIOD.
Think of railway platforms: every train on Platform 1 heads the same way - the platform tells you the family.
A group is a platform: its elements share a chemical destination, meaning similar behaviour.
A period is more like the order in which platforms fill up as the station expands.
How the table was built: three leaps
Leap 1 - patterns in small clusters: Doebereiner's triads, Newlands' octaves, the telluric helix, the atomic-volume curve.
Leap 2 - Mendeleev arranges all known elements by atomic weight and boldly leaves gaps for the undiscovered.
Leap 3 - Moseley's correction: the true organising principle is atomic number, not atomic weight.

segments.text: Before we go anywhere, we need to read the map. The periodic table has two directions, and each one means something very specific.
A vertical column is called a group. A horizontal row is called a period. Those two words will follow you through the entire chapter, so lock them in now.

Here is a picture for what a group really is. Think of the platforms at a busy junction like Howrah or New Delhi. Every train on Platform one heads north; every train on Platform two heads east. You do not read each train's full route - the platform already tells you the family.
A group works exactly like that platform. Every element sitting in it shares a chemical destination - that is, similar behaviour. That shared destination is the reason groups matter so much.
And a period? A period is more like the order in which the platforms fill up as the station keeps expanding - row by row, as elements are added.
<curious>So how did anyone build this map in the first place?</curious> The story is really three big leaps.
The first leap was spotting hidden patterns in small clusters of elements - Doebereiner's triads, Newlands' octaves, de Chancourtois' helix, and Lothar Meyer's curve. Small clues, but real ones.

The second leap was Mendeleev's masterstroke: he arranged all the known elements by atomic weight, and - this is the bold part - he left gaps for elements not yet discovered, and predicted their properties in advance.

The third leap was Moseley's correction. He realised the true organising principle is not atomic weight at all, but atomic number - and that single fix repaired every place where Mendeleev's table had looked wrong.
कहीं जाने से पहले हमें map पढ़नी होगी। Periodic table में दो directions हैं, और हर एक का एक specific मतलब है।
Vertical column को group कहते हैं। Horizontal row को period कहते हैं। ये दो शब्द पूरे chapter में आपके साथ चलेंगे, तो अभी lock कर लो।

Group असल में क्या है, इसकी एक तस्वीर देखो। Howrah या New Delhi जैसे busy junction के platforms सोचो। Platform one की हर train north जाती है; Platform two की हर train east। आप हर train का पूरा route नहीं पढ़ते - platform ही family बता देता है।
Group बिल्कुल उसी platform जैसा काम करता है। उसमें बैठा हर element एक ही chemical destination share करता है - यानी similar behaviour। यही shared destination groups को इतना important बनाता है।
और period? Period ज़्यादा उस order जैसा है जिसमें station बढ़ने पर platforms भरते जाते हैं - row by row, जैसे-जैसे elements add होते हैं।
<curious>तो सबसे पहले ये map बनाई किसने?</curious> कहानी असल में तीन बड़ी leaps की है।
पहली leap थी elements के छोटे clusters में छिपे patterns पकड़ना - Doebereiner की triads, Newlands के octaves, de Chancourtois की helix, और Lothar Meyer की curve। छोटे clues, पर असली।

दूसरी leap थी Mendeleev का masterstroke: उन्होंने सारे known elements को atomic weight से arrange किया, और - यही bold बात है - जो elements अभी discover नहीं हुए थे उनके लिए gaps छोड़ दिए, और पहले ही उनकी properties predict कर दीं।

तीसरी leap थी Moseley की correction। उन्होंने realise किया कि असली organising principle atomic weight नहीं, atomic number है - और इस एक fix ने हर वो जगह ठीक कर दी जहाँ Mendeleev की table गलत दिख रही थी।

sections.title: Early clues: triads and octaves

board_events.text: Early clues: triads and octaves
Doebereiner (1817-1829): in a triad of similar elements ordered by mass, the middle mass is about the average of the other two.
Newlands (1865): order by increasing atomic mass and every eighth element repeats properties - like musical notes.
Newlands' octaves held only up to calcium, then collapsed completely.
Many similar trios are not triads, and octaves fail for heavier elements - these were clues, not laws.
Why examiners love this corner
Every apparent exception is the table being honest about the limits of a simple, early rule.

segments.text: Let's meet the first real clues chemists found. Two of them show up constantly in exams, so we go slowly.

Doebereiner, working between eighteen seventeen and eighteen twenty nine, noticed something neat. Take a group of three chemically similar elements - a triad - and order them by increasing atomic mass. The mass of the middle one is roughly the average of the outer two.
Here is that rule on the board. The middle atomic mass is approximately equal to the first plus the last, divided by two. It is a consistency check, not a deep law - but it works surprisingly often.

Newlands, in eighteen sixty five, spotted a different rhythm. Arrange the elements by increasing atomic mass and every eighth element repeats the properties of the first - like the notes of a musical octave returning to the same note.
<whisper>But here is the catch that examiners live for.</whisper> Newlands' octave pattern held only up to calcium, and then it collapsed completely.
And Doebereiner's triads had their own limit: many similar-looking trios simply are not triads - the averaging fails. So treat both of these as clues, never as universal laws.
This is exactly why examiners love this corner of the chapter.
Every so-called exception you will be asked about is really the periodic table being honest about the limits of a simple, early rule. Keep that framing and the traps stop working on you.
अब उन पहले असली clues से मिलते हैं जो chemists को मिले। इनमें से दो exams में बार-बार आते हैं, तो धीरे चलते हैं।

Doebereiner ने, eighteen seventeen से eighteen twenty nine के बीच, एक neat चीज़ notice की। तीन chemically similar elements का group लो - एक triad - और उन्हें increasing atomic mass से order करो। बीच वाले की mass बाहर वाले दोनों की roughly average होती है।
ये rule board पर देखो। Middle atomic mass approximately बराबर है first plus last का, divided by two। ये एक consistency check है, deep law नहीं - पर काम हैरानी की हद तक अक्सर करता है।

Newlands ने, eighteen sixty five में, एक अलग rhythm पकड़ी। Elements को increasing atomic mass से arrange करो, तो हर आठवाँ element पहले की properties दोहराता है - जैसे musical octave के notes वापस उसी note पर आते हैं।
<whisper>पर यहाँ वो catch है जिसके लिए examiners जीते हैं।</whisper> Newlands का octave pattern सिर्फ calcium तक चला, और फिर पूरी तरह collapse हो गया।
और Doebereiner की triads की अपनी limit थी: कई similar दिखने वाले trios असल में triads हैं ही नहीं - averaging fail कर जाती है। तो इन दोनों को clues मानो, कभी universal laws नहीं।
इसीलिए examiners को chapter का ये कोना बहुत पसंद है।
जो भी so-called exception आपसे पूछा जाएगा, वो असल में periodic table का एक simple, early rule की limits के बारे में ईमानदार होना है। यही framing रखो और traps काम करना बंद कर देंगे।

sections.title: Mendeleev's law and the Moseley correction

board_events.text: Two laws, one crucial swap
Mendeleev's Periodic Law (1869): properties are a periodic function of atomic WEIGHT.
Modern Periodic Law (Moseley, ~1913): properties are a periodic function of atomic NUMBER (Z).
The lock: Mendeleev = weight; Modern = number. Swapping these is the single most-penalised slip.
Mendeleev's law quietly assumed atomic weight was the master variable.
That assumption cracks at a few stubborn pairs - argon and potassium, tellurium and iodine, cobalt and nickel.
Ordering by atomic number Z makes those cracks disappear - no hand-corrections needed.
Why the swap is deep, not cosmetic
Chemistry is run by electrons; the electron count is fixed by Z - so Z, not weight, is the honest ruler.

segments.text: Now the heart of the subtopic - two laws that look almost identical in words, but differ in one crucial variable.
Mendeleev's Periodic Law, from eighteen sixty nine, says the physical and chemical properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.
The Modern Periodic Law, from Moseley around nineteen thirteen, changes exactly one word: properties are a periodic function of their atomic numbers, the quantity we write as Z.
<whisper>Lock this pair right now.</whisper> Mendeleev equals weight; modern equals number. Swapping these two is the single most-penalised mistake in the whole chapter.
Why does the swap even matter? Mendeleev's law quietly assumed that atomic weight was the master variable - the thing that truly ordered the elements.
But that assumption cracks at a few stubborn pairs. Argon and potassium, tellurium and iodine, cobalt and nickel - in each case, ordering strictly by weight puts the wrong element first.
Re-order those same pairs by atomic number Z, and the cracks simply vanish. No manual swaps, no apologies - the sequence just comes out right.
So is this a cosmetic change or a deep one? It is deep.
Chemistry is run by electrons, and the number of electrons in a neutral atom is fixed by Z, the proton count. That is why Z, and not weight, is the honest ruler for the table.
अब subtopic का दिल - दो laws जो शब्दों में लगभग एक जैसी दिखती हैं, पर एक crucial variable में फर्क रखती हैं।
Mendeleev की Periodic Law, eighteen sixty nine से, कहती है कि elements की physical और chemical properties उनके atomic weights का periodic function हैं।
Modern Periodic Law, Moseley की, करीब nineteen thirteen से, बस एक शब्द बदलती है: properties atomic numbers का periodic function हैं - वही quantity जिसे हम Z लिखते हैं।
<whisper>इस pair को अभी lock करो।</whisper> Mendeleev मतलब weight; modern मतलब number। इन दोनों को swap करना पूरे chapter की सबसे ज़्यादा penalise होने वाली गलती है।
ये swap matter ही क्यों करता है? Mendeleev की law चुपचाप मान लेती थी कि atomic weight ही master variable है - वो चीज़ जो सच में elements को order करती है।
पर वो assumption कुछ stubborn pairs पर crack कर जाती है। Argon और potassium, tellurium और iodine, cobalt और nickel - हर case में सिर्फ weight से order करने पर गलत element पहले आ जाता है।
उन्हीं pairs को atomic number Z से re-order करो, और cracks गायब हो जाती हैं। कोई manual swap नहीं, कोई सफाई नहीं - sequence अपने आप सही निकलती है।
तो ये cosmetic change है या deep? ये deep है।
Chemistry electrons से चलती है, और neutral atom में electrons की संख्या Z यानी proton count से fix होती है। इसीलिए table के लिए Z ईमानदार ruler है, weight नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Development of the Periodic Table & the Modern Periodic Law
sections.title: Reading the table: period, group, atomic number

board_events.text: Three core definitions
Period - a horizontal row. Same period means the same number of occupied principal shells (same highest n). There are 7 periods.
Group - a vertical column. Same group means a similar valence-shell configuration, hence similar chemistry. The long form has 18 groups.
Atomic number Z - the proton count (equals electrons in a neutral atom). It defines the element's identity.
How many elements fit in each period
These counts come from the subshells filled: $1s$; $2s\,2p$; $3s\,3p$; $4s\,3d\,4p$; $5s\,4d\,5p$; $6s\,4f\,5d\,6p$; $7s\,5f\,6d\,7p$.
These magic numbers are a consequence of subshell capacities - not coincidence.

segments.text: Three definitions carry the rest of the chapter. Get them crisp and everything downstream is easier.

First, a period is a horizontal row. Elements in the same period share the same number of occupied principal energy shells - the same highest principal quantum number, n. There are seven periods in all.

Second, a group is a vertical column. Elements in the same group share a similar valence-shell electronic configuration, and that is precisely why they behave alike chemically. The modern long form has eighteen groups, numbered one to eighteen.
Third, and most fundamental, atomic number Z is the number of protons - which, in a neutral atom, equals the number of electrons. Z is what actually defines an element's identity.
Now, how many elements can each period hold? The pattern is worth memorising.
Two, eight, eight, eighteen, eighteen, thirty two, thirty two - those are the capacities of periods one through seven.

And they are not random. They come straight from which subshells fill in each period: just one s subshell in period one, then s and p, then the d subshell joins in period four, and the f subshell in period six.
<excited>So those magic numbers - two, eight, eight, eighteen and so on - are a direct consequence of subshell capacities, not a coincidence you have to memorise blindly.</excited>
तीन definitions बाकी पूरे chapter को उठाती हैं। इन्हें crisp कर लो और आगे सब कुछ आसान हो जाता है।
पहली, period एक horizontal row है। एक ही period के elements में occupied principal energy shells की संख्या same होती है - यानी same highest principal quantum number, n। कुल सात periods हैं।

दूसरी, group एक vertical column है। एक ही group के elements की valence-shell electronic configuration similar होती है, और इसीलिए उनकी chemistry एक जैसी होती है। Modern long form में अठारह groups हैं, one to eighteen numbered।
तीसरी, और सबसे fundamental, atomic number Z protons की संख्या है - जो neutral atom में electrons की संख्या के बराबर होती है। Z ही असल में element की identity define करता है।
अब, हर period में कितने elements आ सकते हैं? ये pattern याद रखने लायक है।
Two, eight, eight, eighteen, eighteen, thirty two, thirty two - ये periods one से seven तक की capacities हैं।

और ये random नहीं हैं। ये सीधे इससे आती हैं कि हर period में कौन-से subshells भरते हैं: period one में सिर्फ एक s subshell, फिर s और p, फिर period four में d subshell जुड़ता है, और period six में f subshell।
<excited>तो वो magic numbers - two, eight, eight, eighteen वगैरह - subshell capacities का सीधा नतीजा हैं, कोई coincidence नहीं जिसे आँख मूँदकर रटना पड़े।</excited>

sections.subtopic: Development of the Periodic Table & the Modern Periodic Law
sections.title: Mendeleev's crystal ball: predicting the eka-elements

board_events.text: Mendeleev's crystal ball: the eka-elements
He left a gap below aluminium (eka-aluminium) and below silicon (eka-silicon) and predicted their properties in advance.
For eka-silicon he predicted an oxide of form $EO_2$ and a chloride $ECl_4$.
Germanium delivered exactly $GeO_2$ and $GeCl_4$ - with density and atomic mass close to prediction.
Gallium filled the eka-aluminium slot; germanium filled eka-silicon. The matches were striking.
Why interpolation was allowed to work
If properties vary smoothly down a group and across a period, a missing slot must hold an element intermediate between its known neighbours.

segments.text: Now for the most dramatic moment in the whole story - Mendeleev's crystal ball.

Instead of forcing every known element into a slot, he did something bold: he left gaps. He left an empty space below aluminium, which he called eka-aluminium, and one below silicon, eka-silicon - and then he predicted the properties of those missing elements before anyone had found them.
For eka-silicon, for instance, he predicted the oxide would have the form E O two and the chloride E C l four, where E stands for the unknown element.
Here is that prediction written out - an oxide E O two and a chloride E C l four.

<excited>And when germanium was finally discovered, it delivered exactly germanium dioxide and germanium tetrachloride - with a measured density and atomic mass strikingly close to what he had predicted.</excited>
Gallium turned out to be the eka-aluminium he had described, and germanium the eka-silicon. Two predictions, two direct hits - that is what turned a clever table into a trusted law.
So why was such interpolation even allowed to work?

Because properties vary smoothly as you move down a group and across a period. A missing slot is boxed in by known neighbours, so its properties must sit between theirs. Mendeleev simply read off the trend and filled the gap.
अब पूरी कहानी का सबसे dramatic moment - Mendeleev का crystal ball।

हर known element को किसी slot में ठूँसने की बजाय, उन्होंने एक bold काम किया: उन्होंने gaps छोड़े। Aluminium के नीचे एक खाली जगह छोड़ी, जिसे eka-aluminium कहा, और silicon के नीचे एक, eka-silicon - और फिर उन missing elements की properties predict कर दीं, इससे पहले कि कोई उन्हें ढूँढ़ पाता।
जैसे eka-silicon के लिए उन्होंने predict किया कि oxide का form E O two होगा और chloride E C l four, जहाँ E उस unknown element को दर्शाता है।
ये रही वो prediction लिखी हुई - एक oxide E O two और एक chloride E C l four।

<excited>और जब germanium आखिरकार discover हुआ, तो उसने बिल्कुल वही दिया - germanium dioxide और germanium tetrachloride - measured density और atomic mass उसकी prediction के हैरान करने वाले करीब।</excited>
Gallium वही eka-aluminium निकला जिसका उन्होंने वर्णन किया था, और germanium वही eka-silicon। दो predictions, दो direct hits - यही वो चीज़ थी जिसने एक clever table को trusted law बना दिया।
तो ऐसी interpolation काम करने की इजाज़त ही क्यों मिली?

क्योंकि group में नीचे जाते हुए और period में across जाते हुए properties smoothly बदलती हैं। एक missing slot known neighbours के बीच घिरा होता है, तो उसकी properties उन्हीं के बीच बैठनी चाहिए। Mendeleev ने बस trend पढ़ा और gap भर दिया।

board_events.text: Naming elements with Z greater than 100
For $Z \gt 100$, IUPAC builds a temporary name digit-by-digit from numerical roots.
Roots - 0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn.
Procedure: write Z digit by digit, swap each digit for its root, join in order, then add the ending -ium.
The symbol is the first letter of each root, capitalising only the first.
Sanity check: a three-digit Z always gives a three-letter symbol; always read the digits left to right.
This exact digit-by-digit skill shows up in JEE Main, often stitched to block prediction.

segments.text: Here is a small but reliable scoring skill: naming the superheavy elements, the ones with atomic number greater than one hundred.
For any element with Z above one hundred, I U P A C gives it a temporary systematic name, built digit by digit from a set of numerical roots.
The roots are worth memorising: zero is nil, one is un, two is bi, three is tri, four is quad, five is pent, six is hex, seven is sept, eight is oct, and nine is enn.
The procedure is mechanical. Write the atomic number digit by digit, replace each digit by its root, join the roots in order, and finish with the ending spoken as ium.
The symbol follows the same digits: take the first letter of each root, and capitalise only the very first letter.
Let's do one hundred twenty four. Its digits are one, two, four - that is un, bi, quad - joined and given the ium ending gives unbiquadium, with the symbol U b q.
<whisper>Here is a quick sanity check.</whisper> A three-digit atomic number always produces a three-letter symbol, and you must always read the digits strictly left to right - never reverse them.
This exact skill turns up in J E E Main, very often stitched together with predicting which block the element belongs to - so it is worth being fluent.
ये एक छोटी पर भरोसेमंद scoring skill है: superheavy elements को name देना, वो जिनका atomic number एक सौ से ज़्यादा है।
जिस भी element का Z एक सौ से ऊपर है, I U P A C उसे एक temporary systematic name देता है, जो numerical roots के set से digit by digit बनता है।
Roots याद रखने लायक हैं: zero है nil, one है un, two है bi, three है tri, four है quad, five है pent, six है hex, seven है sept, eight है oct, और nine है enn।
Procedure mechanical है। Atomic number को digit by digit लिखो, हर digit को उसके root से replace करो, roots को order में जोड़ो, और अंत में ending लगाओ जिसे ium बोलते हैं।
Symbol उन्हीं digits से बनता है: हर root का पहला letter लो, और सिर्फ सबसे पहले letter को capital करो।
एक सौ चौबीस करके देखते हैं। इसके digits हैं one, two, four - यानी un, bi, quad - जोड़कर और ium ending देकर बनता है unbiquadium, symbol U b q।
<whisper>एक quick sanity check।</whisper> तीन-digit वाला atomic number हमेशा तीन-letter का symbol देता है, और digits को हमेशा left to right पढ़ना है - कभी उल्टा नहीं।
ये exact skill J E E Main में आती है, अक्सर इसके साथ जोड़कर कि element किस block में है - तो इसमें fluent होना फायदेमंद है।

sections.title: From atomic weight to atomic number: the reasoning chain

board_events.text: The reasoning chain: weight to number
Step 1 - Anomalies. By weight, argon (~40) lands after potassium (~39), placing a noble gas among reactive metals. Chemically absurd.
The same trouble hits tellurium/iodine and cobalt/nickel; Mendeleev had to swap them by hand.
Step 2 - A deeper variable is needed. Chemistry is set by electrons, and electron count is fixed by nuclear charge (protons).
Step 3 - Moseley's evidence: characteristic X-ray spectra gave a clean whole-number quantity - the atomic number Z.
Step 4 - Order by Z and the anomalies dissolve: $Z_{Ar}=18 \lt Z_{K}=19$, $Z_{Te}=52 \lt Z_{I}=53$, $Z_{Co}=27 \lt Z_{Ni}=28$.
Argon outweighs potassium only because it is neutron-rich (its mass-40 isotope dominates).
The takeaway
Weight counts total nucleons and wobbles with isotopes; Z counts protons and fixes chemistry. Z is the more fundamental ruler.

segments.text: This is the conceptual spine of the subtopic - the chain of reasoning that took chemists from atomic weight to atomic number. Four clean steps.

Step one, the anomalies. If you order strictly by atomic weight, argon, at about forty, lands after potassium, at about thirty nine. That drops argon, a noble gas, right into the column of reactive metals. Chemically, that is absurd.

The same trouble shows up at tellurium and iodine, and at cobalt and nickel. In every case Mendeleev had to reach in and swap the pair by hand to keep the chemistry sensible - effectively admitting his own law had cracks.

Step two: a deeper variable is needed. Chemistry is governed by electrons, and the number of electrons is set by the nuclear charge - the number of protons. So maybe the proton count, not the weight, is what really orders the elements.

Step three, Moseley's evidence. Studying the characteristic X ray spectra of the elements, Moseley found a clean, regular relationship tied to a whole-number quantity - the atomic number Z - and proposed Z as the true ordering variable.

<excited>Step four, and everything clicks.</excited> Order by Z and the anomalies dissolve: argon's eighteen comes before potassium's nineteen, tellurium's fifty two before iodine's fifty three, cobalt's twenty seven before nickel's twenty eight. No hand-swaps needed.

But why is argon heavier than potassium at all, despite fewer protons? Because atomic mass counts neutrons too. Natural argon is dominated by its mass-forty isotope, which is neutron-rich, so it out-weighs potassium even with one fewer proton.
So here is the takeaway to carry forward.
Atomic weight counts total nucleons and wobbles with isotopes; atomic number counts protons and fixes the chemistry. That is why Z is the more fundamental, anomaly-free ruler for the table.
ये subtopic की conceptual रीढ़ है - वो reasoning chain जो chemists को atomic weight से atomic number तक ले गई। चार साफ steps।

Step one, anomalies। अगर सिर्फ atomic weight से order करो, तो argon, करीब forty पर, potassium के बाद आता है, जो करीब thirty nine पर है। इससे argon, एक noble gas, सीधे reactive metals के column में गिर जाता है। Chemically ये absurd है।
वही मुसीबत tellurium और iodine पर, और cobalt और nickel पर आती है। हर case में Mendeleev को हाथ से pair swap करना पड़ा ताकि chemistry सही रहे - यानी उन्होंने खुद माना कि उनकी law में cracks हैं।

Step two: एक deeper variable चाहिए। Chemistry electrons से चलती है, और electrons की संख्या nuclear charge - यानी protons की संख्या - से set होती है। तो शायद proton count, weight नहीं, असल में elements को order करता है।

Step three, Moseley की evidence। Elements के characteristic X ray spectra study करके, Moseley को एक clean, regular relationship मिला जो एक whole-number quantity से जुड़ा था - atomic number Z - और उन्होंने Z को असली ordering variable proposed किया।

<excited>Step four, और सब कुछ जगह पर आ जाता है।</excited> Z से order करो और anomalies घुल जाती हैं: argon का eighteen potassium के nineteen से पहले, tellurium का fifty two iodine के fifty three से पहले, cobalt का twenty seven nickel के twenty eight से पहले। कोई hand-swap नहीं।

पर argon potassium से भारी है ही क्यों, कम protons के बावजूद? क्योंकि atomic mass neutrons को भी गिनती है। Natural argon में उसका mass-forty isotope dominate करता है, जो neutron-rich है, तो एक कम proton होने पर भी वो potassium से भारी निकलता है।
तो ये रहा आगे ले जाने वाला takeaway।
Atomic weight total nucleons गिनती है और isotopes के साथ डगमगाती है; atomic number protons गिनता है और chemistry fix करता है। इसीलिए Z table के लिए ज़्यादा fundamental, anomaly-free ruler है।

board_events.text: Building and reading the long form
The row you are in = the highest principal quantum number n being filled = the period.
The subshell that receives the last (differentiating) electron sets your block: s, p, d, or f.
The valence-shell configuration fixes the group; the same valence configuration means group-mates.

The metal / metalloid / non-metal boundary is the staircase running through the p-block.
Why this matters
Once you can read row, block, and valence configuration, you can place almost any element without memorising the chart.

segments.text: Let's put it all together and actually read the long form of the table - the version you will see on every exam wall.
First, the row you are in equals the highest principal quantum number, n, that is being filled. That number is your period. Simple as that.

Second, the subshell that receives the last electron - the differentiating electron - sets your block. If it lands in an s subshell you are in the s-block; in p, the p-block; in d, the d-block; in f, the f-block.
Third, the valence-shell configuration fixes your group. Two elements with the same valence configuration are group-mates, and that is exactly why they share chemistry.

Look at the figure. The table splits into four coloured regions. On the far left, two columns of s-block. On the far right, six columns of p-block. Tucked in the centre, ten columns of d-block. And pulled out below, the fourteen-wide f-block.

<curious>Notice how the widths tell a story?</curious> The s-block is groups one and two, the p-block is groups thirteen to eighteen, the d-block is groups three to twelve, and the f-block is printed separately below to keep the chart a sensible width.
Running diagonally through the p-block is the staircase - the boundary that separates metals from non-metals, with the metalloids sitting right along the steps.
Why does all of this matter so much?

Because once you can read the row, the block, and the valence configuration, you can place almost any element on the table without memorising the chart at all - you derive its address instead of recalling it.
अब सब कुछ जोड़कर table की long form असल में पढ़ते हैं - वही version जो हर exam की दीवार पर दिखता है।
पहला, जिस row में आप हो वो highest principal quantum number, n, के बराबर है जो भर रहा है। वही number आपका period है। बस इतना ही।
दूसरा, जो subshell आखिरी electron - differentiating electron - लेता है, वो आपका block set करता है। अगर वो s subshell में गिरे तो s-block; p में तो p-block; d में तो d-block; f में तो f-block।
तीसरा, valence-shell configuration आपका group fix करता है। same valence configuration वाले दो elements group-mates होते हैं, और इसीलिए उनकी chemistry एक जैसी होती है।

Figure देखो। Table चार coloured regions में बँटती है। बाईं ओर, s-block के दो columns। दाईं ओर, p-block के छह columns। बीच में tucked, d-block के दस columns। और नीचे अलग निकाला हुआ, चौदह चौड़ा f-block।

<curious>ध्यान दो कैसे widths एक कहानी कहती हैं?</curious> s-block groups one और two है, p-block groups thirteen से eighteen, d-block groups three से twelve, और f-block नीचे अलग print होता है ताकि chart की width sensible रहे।
P-block में diagonally गुज़रती है staircase - वो boundary जो metals को non-metals से अलग करती है, और metalloids ठीक उन steps पर बैठते हैं।
ये सब इतना matter क्यों करता है?
क्योंकि एक बार आप row, block, और valence configuration पढ़ना सीख जाओ, तो लगभग किसी भी element को table पर बिना chart रटे place कर सकते हो - आप उसका address recall करने की बजाय derive करते हो।

sections.title: Worked example: strontium's mass by the triad rule

board_events.text: Worked Example: predict strontium's atomic mass
Given: calcium mass = 40.1 u, barium mass = 137.3 u. Strontium lies between them in a Doebereiner triad.
Predicted strontium mass is about 88.7 u.
The accepted value is 87.6 u - the prediction is within about 1.3%.
Close agreement confirms calcium, strontium, barium form a valid triad.
The exam lesson
A triad estimate is a consistency check: a close match supports the triad; a large gap means the grouping fails.

segments.text: Let's put the triad rule to work on a classic C B S E board question.

We are given calcium with atomic mass forty point one, and barium with atomic mass one hundred thirty seven point three. Strontium sits between them in a Doebereiner triad, and we want to predict its mass.
The triad rule says the middle mass is approximately the average of the outer two - so strontium's mass is about calcium plus barium, all over two.
Plug in the numbers: forty point one plus one hundred thirty seven point three is one hundred seventy seven point four; divide by two and we get eighty eight point seven.
So the predicted atomic mass of strontium is about eighty eight point seven units.
<excited>Now compare with reality: the accepted value is eighty seven point six units - our prediction is off by only about one point three percent.</excited>
That close agreement is the point. It confirms that calcium, strontium, and barium really do form a valid Doebereiner triad.
And here is the exam lesson tucked inside this example.
A triad estimate is a consistency check, not a law. A close match supports the triad; a large gap would tell you the three elements are not a genuine triad at all.
चलो triad rule को एक classic C B S E board question पर काम में लगाते हैं।

हमें दिया है calcium जिसकी atomic mass forty point one है, और barium जिसकी one hundred thirty seven point three। Strontium इनके बीच एक Doebereiner triad में बैठता है, और हमें उसकी mass predict करनी है।
Triad rule कहता है कि middle mass बाहर वाले दोनों की approximately average होती है - तो strontium की mass करीब calcium plus barium, whole over two है।
Numbers डालो: forty point one plus one hundred thirty seven point three बराबर one hundred seventy seven point four; two से divide करो तो मिलता है eighty eight point seven।
तो strontium की predicted atomic mass करीब eighty eight point seven units है।
<excited>अब reality से मिलाओ: accepted value है eighty seven point six units - हमारी prediction सिर्फ करीब one point three percent off है।</excited>
यही close agreement असली बात है। ये confirm करती है कि calcium, strontium, और barium सच में एक valid Doebereiner triad बनाते हैं।
और इस example के अंदर छिपा exam lesson ये है।
Triad estimate एक consistency check है, law नहीं। Close match triad को support करता है; बड़ा gap बता देता कि तीनों elements असल में triad हैं ही नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Development of the Periodic Table & the Modern Periodic Law
sections.title: Worked example: spotting false universals (NEET)

board_events.text: Worked Example: how many statements are correct?
Statement I: Newlands' octaves stayed valid up to and beyond iron.
Statement II: Doebereiner's mass-rule applies to every set of three similar elements.
Statement III: Mendeleev arranged elements primarily by atomic weight.
Do not compute - eliminate on known limits.
I is false: octaves broke down after calcium, not iron.
II is false: many similar trios are not triads - the mean fails.
III is true: that is the textbook statement of Mendeleev's law.
Answer: exactly 1 statement is correct.

segments.text: This one is a N E E T speed trap - a statement question designed to punish over-generalisation. Read each claim and test it against the limits we have built.
Statement one says Newlands' octaves stayed valid up to and beyond iron.
Statement two says Doebereiner's mass-rule applies to every set of three chemically similar elements.
Statement three says Mendeleev arranged the elements primarily by atomic weight.
The question asks how many of these three statements are correct. The trick is to eliminate on known limits, not to compute anything.
<curious>Start with statement one.</curious> This is the classic trap: the octave pattern broke down after calcium, not iron. So statement one is false.
Statement two over-reaches. Many chemically similar trios are simply not triads - the averaging fails for them - so a rule that claims to apply to every such set is false.
Statement three, though, is just the textbook definition of Mendeleev's law, arranging by atomic weight. That one is true.

So exactly one statement is correct. Notice how both wrong options work the same way - they take a limited historical pattern and dress it up as a universal law. That is the most common way this topic is trapped.
ये एक N E E T speed trap है - एक statement question जो over-generalisation को सज़ा देने के लिए बना है। हर claim पढ़ो और उसे हमारी बनाई limits से test करो।
Statement one कहता है कि Newlands के octaves iron तक और उससे आगे valid रहे।
Statement two कहता है कि Doebereiner का mass-rule हर तीन chemically similar elements के set पर लागू होता है।
Statement three कहता है कि Mendeleev ने elements को मुख्यतः atomic weight से arrange किया।
सवाल है कि इन तीन में से कितने statements सही हैं। Trick ये है कि known limits पर eliminate करो, कुछ compute मत करो।
<curious>Statement one से शुरू करो।</curious> ये classic trap है: octave pattern calcium के बाद टूटा, iron के बाद नहीं। तो statement one false है।
Statement two ज़्यादा दावा करता है। कई chemically similar trios असल में triads हैं ही नहीं - उनके लिए averaging fail हो जाती है - तो एक rule जो हर ऐसे set पर लागू होने का दावा करे, false है।
पर statement three बस Mendeleev की law की textbook definition है, atomic weight से arrange करना। वो true है।

तो ठीक एक statement सही है। ध्यान दो कैसे दोनों गलत options एक ही तरीके से काम करते हैं - एक limited historical pattern को उठाकर universal law की तरह पेश कर देते हैं। यही इस topic को trap करने का सबसे common तरीका है।

sections.subtopic: Development of the Periodic Table & the Modern Periodic Law
sections.title: Worked example: name and block for Z = 124 (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Worked Example: name and block for Z = 124
Part (a): give the temporary IUPAC name and symbol for Z = 124.
Digits of 124: 1 to un, 2 to bi, 4 to quad.
Part (b): predict its block, assuming the extended Aufbau order holds.
Oganesson ($Z=118$) is $[Rn]\,5f^{14}\,6d^{10}\,7s^{2}\,7p^{6}$; electrons for 119, 120 enter 8s.
From 121 onward the 5g subshell begins to fill, so $Z=124$ lands in the predicted g-block.
This stitches two skills: digit-by-digit naming and electron-filling logic - a favourite JEE Main combination.

segments.text: Now a J E E Main level question that deliberately stitches two skills together. A newly synthesised superheavy element has atomic number one hundred twenty four.
Part a asks for its temporary I U P A C name and symbol.
Break one hundred twenty four into digits: one, two, four. Convert each to its root - one is un, two is bi, four is quad.
Join the roots and add the ium ending: un, bi, quad, ium gives unbiquadium. Taking the first letter of each root gives the symbol U b q.
Part b asks us to predict its block, assuming the extended Aufbau filling order holds.

Anchor on the last noble gas. Oganesson, at Z equals one hundred eighteen, is a radon core, then five f fourteen, six d ten, seven s two, seven p six. The next electrons, for elements one hundred nineteen and one hundred twenty, enter the eight s subshell.

<curious>And then something new happens.</curious> From element one hundred twenty one onward, the five g subshell begins to fill. So atomic number one hundred twenty four lands in the predicted g-block - a hypothetical extension beyond the current s, p, d, f scheme.
This is exactly the kind of stitching J E E Main loves: the mechanical naming procedure on one side, and electron-filling logic on the other, folded into a single question.
अब एक J E E Main level question जो जानबूझकर दो skills को साथ जोड़ता है। एक नया synthesise हुआ superheavy element है जिसका atomic number एक सौ चौबीस है।
Part a माँगता है इसका temporary I U P A C name और symbol।
एक सौ चौबीस को digits में तोड़ो: one, two, four। हर एक को उसके root में बदलो - one है un, two है bi, four है quad।
Roots जोड़ो और ium ending लगाओ: un, bi, quad, ium बनता है unbiquadium। हर root का पहला letter लेने से symbol U b q मिलता है।
Part b कहता है इसका block predict करो, ये मानते हुए कि extended Aufbau filling order चलता है।

आखिरी noble gas पर anchor करो। Oganesson, Z बराबर एक सौ अठारह पर, एक radon core है, फिर five f fourteen, six d ten, seven s two, seven p six। अगले electrons, elements एक सौ उन्नीस और एक सौ बीस के लिए, eight s subshell में जाते हैं।

<curious>और फिर कुछ नया होता है।</curious> Element एक सौ इक्कीस से आगे, five g subshell भरना शुरू होता है। तो atomic number एक सौ चौबीस predicted g-block में गिरता है - मौजूदा s, p, d, f scheme से आगे का एक hypothetical extension।
ये ठीक वैसी stitching है जो J E E Main को पसंद है: एक तरफ mechanical naming procedure, दूसरी तरफ electron-filling logic, एक ही question में मोड़ी हुई।

sections.subtopic: Development of the Periodic Table & the Modern Periodic Law
sections.title: Worked example: argon before potassium (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: Worked Example: why argon precedes potassium
Argon ($Z=18$, mass ~ 39.95) precedes potassium ($Z=19$, mass ~ 39.10) - yet argon is heavier.
(a) A strict weight ordering would invert the pair: argon, a noble gas, would sit in the reactive-metal column.
The modern law orders by Z: $Z_{Ar}=18 \lt Z_{K}=19$, so argon precedes potassium automatically.
(b) Why is argon heavier despite fewer protons? Atomic mass depends on neutrons too.
Natural argon is dominated by its mass-40 isotope (neutron-rich); potassium's main isotope is mass-39.
So argon carries more nucleons on average, even with one fewer proton.
The limitation this exposes
Weight tracks total nucleon count (isotope-dependent); chemistry tracks electron count, fixed by Z. Hence Z is more fundamental.

segments.text: Let's finish the worked examples with a J E E Advanced question that ties the whole subtopic together.

The situation: argon, atomic number eighteen with mass about thirty nine point nine five, appears before potassium, atomic number nineteen with mass about thirty nine point one zero. And yet argon is the heavier of the two.

Part a. Under a strict atomic-weight ordering, the heavier argon would be placed after potassium - which drops a noble gas straight into the reactive-metal column, and pushes potassium in among the inert gases. Chemically absurd, so Mendeleev had to invert the pair by hand.

<whisper>The modern law needs no such rescue.</whisper> It orders by atomic number, and since argon's eighteen is less than potassium's nineteen, argon automatically comes first, each element landing in its correct chemical family.
Part b asks the deeper question: why is argon heavier at all, when it has one fewer proton? The answer is that atomic mass depends on neutrons too, not just protons.
Naturally occurring argon is dominated by its mass-forty isotope, which is relatively neutron-rich, while potassium's principal isotope has mass thirty nine.
So argon, despite one fewer proton, carries more nucleons on average - and that makes it heavier.
And here is the limitation this whole episode exposes.

Atomic weight tracks the total nucleon count, which wobbles with isotopes and neutron number; chemical behaviour tracks the electron count, which is fixed by Z. That is why ordering by Z is both more fundamental and completely free of anomalous pairs.
चलो worked examples को एक J E E Advanced question से खत्म करते हैं जो पूरे subtopic को एक साथ बाँधता है।

स्थिति: argon, atomic number eighteen, mass करीब thirty nine point nine five, potassium से पहले आता है, जो atomic number nineteen, mass करीब thirty nine point one zero है। और फिर भी argon दोनों में भारी है।

Part a। सख्त atomic-weight ordering में, भारी argon potassium के बाद रखा जाता - जो एक noble gas को सीधे reactive-metal column में गिरा देता, और potassium को inert gases के बीच धकेल देता। Chemically absurd, तो Mendeleev को pair हाथ से invert करना पड़ा।

<whisper>Modern law को ऐसी किसी rescue की ज़रूरत नहीं।</whisper> ये atomic number से order करती है, और चूँकि argon का eighteen potassium के nineteen से कम है, argon अपने आप पहले आता है, हर element अपनी सही chemical family में गिरता है।
Part b गहरा सवाल पूछता है: argon भारी है ही क्यों, जब उसमें एक कम proton है? जवाब ये है कि atomic mass neutrons पर भी depend करती है, सिर्फ protons पर नहीं।
Naturally occurring argon में उसका mass-forty isotope dominate करता है, जो relatively neutron-rich है, जबकि potassium के principal isotope की mass thirty nine है।
तो argon, एक कम proton के बावजूद, average में ज़्यादा nucleons रखता है - और यही उसे भारी बनाता है।
और ये पूरा episode जो limitation उजागर करता है, वो ये है।

Atomic weight total nucleon count track करती है, जो isotopes और neutron number के साथ डगमगाती है; chemical behaviour electron count track करती है, जो Z से fix होती है। इसीलिए Z से order करना ज़्यादा fundamental भी है और anomalous pairs से पूरी तरह free भी।

sections.subtopic: Development of the Periodic Table & the Modern Periodic Law
sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Common pitfalls and pro-tips
Pitfall 1: swapping the two laws' basis. Lock it - Mendeleev = weight, Modern (Moseley) = number.
Pitfall 2: treating triads and octaves as universal. Octaves die after calcium; many trios are not triads.
Pitfall 3: nomenclature slips - forgetting the -ium ending, confusing roots, or reversing digit order.
Pitfall 4: calling anomalous pairs 'Mendeleev's mistakes'. They are evidence that weight was the wrong variable.
Pro-tip: memorise the chronology as one chain - Doebereiner, Newlands, de Chancourtois / Lothar Meyer, Mendeleev, Moseley.
Attach one keyword each: triads, octaves, helix / curve, gaps and weight, number. Most one-markers fall off this chain.
For nomenclature, sanity-check symbol length: a three-digit Z always gives a three-letter symbol.

segments.text: Before we close the subtopic, let's gather the pitfalls that cost marks and the pro-tips that save time.

<whisper>Pitfall one is the most penalised error in the entire chapter.</whisper> Do not swap the basis of the two laws. Lock it in: Mendeleev equals weight, and the modern law, Moseley's, equals number.

Pitfall two: treating triads and octaves as universal truths. They are narrow historical clues - octaves die after calcium, and many chemically similar trios are simply not triads. Examiners trap this constantly.
Pitfall three: nomenclature slips. Forgetting the ium ending, confusing quad with a similar-sounding root, or reversing the digit order. Always read the atomic number left to right, root by root.

Pitfall four: calling the anomalous pairs Mendeleev's mistakes. They are not errors at all - they are the evidence that atomic weight was the wrong variable, with neutron count and isotopes explaining the heavier-but-earlier ordering.
Now the pro-tips. Memorise the chronology as a single chain: Doebereiner, Newlands, de Chancourtois and Lothar Meyer, Mendeleev, and finally Moseley.

Attach one keyword to each link - triads, octaves, helix and curve, gaps and weight, and number. Most N E E T and board one-markers are answered straight off this chain, with no real reasoning needed.

And for naming questions, sanity-check the symbol length before you commit: a three-digit atomic number always produces a three-letter symbol. If your symbol has the wrong length, you have slipped somewhere.
Subtopic बंद करने से पहले, चलो वो pitfalls इकट्ठा करते हैं जो marks खाते हैं और वो pro-tips जो time बचाते हैं।
<whisper>Pitfall one पूरे chapter की सबसे ज़्यादा penalise होने वाली गलती है।</whisper> दोनों laws का basis swap मत करो। Lock कर लो: Mendeleev बराबर weight, और modern law, Moseley की, बराबर number।

Pitfall two: triads और octaves को universal सच मानना। ये narrow historical clues हैं - octaves calcium के बाद मर जाते हैं, और कई chemically similar trios असल में triads हैं ही नहीं। Examiners इसे बार-बार trap करते हैं।
Pitfall three: nomenclature slips। ium ending भूल जाना, quad को किसी similar-sounding root से confuse करना, या digit order उल्टा कर देना। Atomic number को हमेशा left to right, root by root पढ़ो।

Pitfall four: anomalous pairs को Mendeleev की गलतियाँ कहना। ये errors हैं ही नहीं - ये वो evidence हैं कि atomic weight गलत variable था, जहाँ neutron count और isotopes उस heavier-but-earlier ordering को समझाते हैं।
अब pro-tips। Chronology को एक single chain की तरह याद करो: Doebereiner, Newlands, de Chancourtois और Lothar Meyer, Mendeleev, और आखिर में Moseley।
हर link पर एक keyword चिपकाओ - triads, octaves, helix और curve, gaps और weight, और number। ज़्यादातर N E E T और board one-markers इसी chain से सीधे answer हो जाते हैं, बिना किसी real reasoning के।

और naming questions के लिए, commit करने से पहले symbol length की sanity-check करो: तीन-digit वाला atomic number हमेशा तीन-letter का symbol देता है। अगर आपके symbol की length गलत है, तो कहीं slip हुई है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: The master engine: effective nuclear charge

board_events.text: The two forces behind every trend
Once an element has its seat, we predict its size, its grip on electrons, and its pull on shared pairs.
Picture a crowded train compartment with one ticket-checker at the door - that is the nucleus.
Valence electrons near the door feel his authority; inner electrons block his view - that is shielding.
What a valence electron truly feels is the effective nuclear charge, $Z_{\text{eff}}$.
Here $\sigma$ is screening from inner electrons. Hold onto $Z_{\text{eff}}$ - it is the engine under every trend.
Almost every physical trend is just a tug-of-war between nuclear pull and electron shielding.

segments.text: In the last subtopic we settled what organises the table - the atomic number. Now we ask the far more useful question: once an element has its seat, can we predict how it behaves physically?
Specifically, three things. How big is the atom, how tightly does it grip its own electrons, and how greedily does it pull on a shared pair? Remarkably, almost all of it comes down to one quantity.

<curious>Here is the picture I want in your head.</curious> Imagine a crowded local train compartment with a single ticket-checker standing at the door. That ticket-checker is the nucleus, and his authority is the nuclear charge.

The passengers nearest the door are the valence electrons - they feel his authority strongly. But the passengers packed between him and the door are the inner-shell electrons, and they block his line of sight, watering down his authority. That blocking is the shielding, or screening, effect.
So what a valence electron actually feels is not the full nuclear charge. It feels a reduced, net pull that we call the effective nuclear charge, written Z effective.
On the board: Z effective equals Z minus sigma.

Here Z is the full nuclear charge and sigma is the screening contributed by the inner electrons. Hold onto this single quantity - Z effective is the engine under the bonnet of every trend we are about to meet.
Because almost every physical trend in the table is just a tug-of-war between two opposing forces: the nucleus pulling electrons in, and the inner electrons shielding them from that pull.

पिछले subtopic में हमने तय किया कि table को organise क्या करता है - atomic number। अब हम कहीं ज़्यादा useful सवाल पूछते हैं: एक बार element को उसकी seat मिल जाए, तो क्या हम predict कर सकते हैं कि वो physically कैसा behave करेगा?
खास तौर पर तीन चीज़ें। Atom कितना बड़ा है, अपने electrons को कितनी tightly पकड़ता है, और shared pair को कितनी greedily खींचता है? हैरानी की बात, ये लगभग सब कुछ एक ही quantity पर टिका है।

<curious>ये तस्वीर आपके दिमाग में चाहिए।</curious> एक भरी हुई local train का compartment सोचो जिसमें दरवाज़े पर एक अकेला ticket-checker खड़ा है। वो ticket-checker nucleus है, और उसकी authority nuclear charge है।

दरवाज़े के सबसे पास वाले passengers valence electrons हैं - वो उसकी authority strongly महसूस करते हैं। पर उसके और दरवाज़े के बीच ठुँसे passengers inner-shell electrons हैं, और वो उसकी नज़र रोक देते हैं, उसकी authority को कमज़ोर कर देते हैं। यही blocking shielding, या screening, effect है।
तो valence electron असल में full nuclear charge महसूस नहीं करता। वो एक reduced, net pull महसूस करता है जिसे हम effective nuclear charge कहते हैं, Z effective लिखते हैं।
Board पर: Z effective बराबर Z minus sigma।
यहाँ Z full nuclear charge है और sigma inner electrons का दिया screening है। इस एक quantity को पकड़े रखो - Z effective हर उस trend का engine है जिससे हम अभी मिलने वाले हैं।
क्योंकि table की लगभग हर physical trend बस दो opposing forces के बीच tug-of-war है: nucleus electrons को अंदर खींच रहा है, और inner electrons उन्हें उस pull से shield कर रहे हैं।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: The mandi walk: how atomic size changes

board_events.text: Walking the mandi: how size changes
Across a period: add a proton AND an electron to the same outer shell.
New electrons shield each other poorly, so $Z_{\text{eff}}$ tightens - atoms SHRINK across a period.
Down a group: a whole new shell opens, farther out, behind a thick inner screen.
Distance and shielding win - atoms GROW down a group.
From this one picture, the rest cascades.
Smaller atom means tighter grip: higher IE, more negative EGE, higher EN.
Across a period: size down, $Z_{\text{eff}}$ up, IE up, EGE more negative, EN up. Down a group: all reverse.

segments.text: Let's turn that engine into a concrete trend using one more everyday picture - shopping in a busy Indian mandi.

Walk across one row of stalls - that is moving across a period. At each step you add both a vendor and a customer at the same counter: in the atom, a proton in the nucleus and an electron in the same outer shell.

But the new electrons are poor at shielding each other, so the nucleus's grip - Z effective - tightens with every step. The cloud of shoppers gets pulled in tighter, and so atoms shrink across a period.
Now walk down to the next floor of the market - that is going down a group. An entirely new shell of stalls opens up, farther from the nucleus, with a thick wall of inner shoppers shielding it.
Here distance and shielding win outright. So atoms grow down a group. Those are the two master directions - shrink across, grow down.
<excited>And from this single picture, the rest of the chapter simply cascades out.</excited>

A smaller atom holds its outer electron more tightly. So it is harder to remove that electron - higher ionisation enthalpy - and more eager to grab an extra one - more negative electron gain enthalpy and higher electronegativity. A bigger atom does the exact opposite.
So memorise one master line. Across a period: size down, Z effective up, ionisation enthalpy up, electron gain enthalpy more negative, electronegativity up. Down a group, every one of those reverses.
चलो उस engine को एक और रोज़मर्रा की तस्वीर से concrete trend में बदलते हैं - एक busy Indian mandi में shopping।

एक row of stalls के across चलो - ये period के across जाना है। हर step पर आप एक ही counter पर एक vendor और एक customer दोनों जोड़ते हो: atom में, nucleus में एक proton और उसी outer shell में एक electron।

पर नए electrons एक-दूसरे को shield करने में कमज़ोर हैं, तो nucleus की पकड़ - Z effective - हर step पर tight होती जाती है। Shoppers का cloud और अंदर खिंच जाता है, और इसलिए period के across atoms सिकुड़ते हैं।
अब market की अगली मंज़िल पर उतरो - ये group में नीचे जाना है। stalls का बिल्कुल नया shell खुलता है, nucleus से दूर, जिसके आगे inner shoppers की मोटी दीवार shield करती है।
यहाँ distance और shielding साफ जीत जाते हैं। तो group में नीचे atoms बड़े होते हैं। यही दो master directions हैं - across सिकुड़ना, down बढ़ना।
<excited>और इस एक तस्वीर से बाकी पूरा chapter बस cascade होकर निकल आता है।</excited>

छोटा atom अपने outer electron को ज़्यादा tightly पकड़ता है। तो उस electron को हटाना मुश्किल - higher ionisation enthalpy - और एक extra पकड़ने को ज़्यादा उत्सुक - more negative electron gain enthalpy और higher electronegativity। बड़ा atom ठीक उल्टा करता है।

तो एक master line याद कर लो। Period के across: size down, Z effective up, ionisation enthalpy up, electron gain enthalpy more negative, electronegativity up। Group में नीचे, इनमें से हर एक reverse हो जाता है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Measuring atomic radius three ways

board_events.text: Measuring atomic radius three ways
An atom has no hard edge - the electron cloud fades - so radius is defined operationally.
Covalent radius: half the internuclear distance between two like atoms in a single bond.
Van der Waals radius: half the distance between non-bonded atoms of adjacent molecules (used for noble gases).
Size order: $r_{vdW} \gt r_{\text{metallic}} \gt r_{\text{cov}}$.
Canonical covalent radii (pm), period 2: Li 152, Be 111, B 88, C 77, N 74, O 66, F 64.
Down group 1 (pm): Li 152, Na 186, K 231, Rb 244, Cs 262 - shrinking across, growing down.

segments.text: Now let's make size measurable. There is a subtlety here that examiners love, so we take it carefully.
<curious>An atom has no hard boundary - the electron cloud just fades away gradually.</curious> So we cannot measure radius with a ruler; we define it operationally, in three different ways.
The first is the covalent radius. Take two identical atoms joined by a single covalent bond, measure the distance between their nuclei, and halve it.
On the board: the covalent radius equals one half of the distance between the two bonded nuclei, d A to A.
The second is the van der Waals radius. For atoms that are not bonded - like noble gases in adjacent molecules - we take half the distance between their nuclei. It is always the largest of the three.

So remember the size order: van der Waals radius is greater than metallic radius, which is greater than covalent radius. Comparing a noble gas's van der Waals radius directly with a neighbour's covalent radius is an apples-to-oranges trap.

Now the canonical data, worth memorising for its shape. Across period two, the covalent radii in picometres run: lithium one hundred fifty two, beryllium one hundred eleven, boron eighty eight, carbon seventy seven, nitrogen seventy four, oxygen sixty six, fluorine sixty four.

And going down group one, in picometres: lithium one hundred fifty two, sodium one hundred eighty six, potassium two hundred thirty one, rubidium two hundred forty four, caesium two hundred sixty two. Shrinking across the period, growing down the group - exactly as the engine predicts.
अब size को measurable बनाते हैं। यहाँ एक subtlety है जो examiners को बहुत पसंद है, तो इसे ध्यान से लेते हैं।
Atom का कोई hard boundary नहीं होता - electron cloud बस धीरे-धीरे fade हो जाता है। तो हम radius को ruler से नहीं माप सकते; हम इसे operationally define करते हैं, तीन अलग तरीकों से।
पहला है covalent radius। दो identical atoms लो जो single covalent bond से जुड़े हों, उनके nuclei के बीच की distance मापो, और आधी कर दो।
Board पर: covalent radius बराबर है दोनों bonded nuclei के बीच की distance, d A to A, का आधा।
दूसरा है van der Waals radius। जो atoms bonded नहीं हैं - जैसे adjacent molecules में noble gases - उनके nuclei के बीच की distance का आधा लेते हैं। ये तीनों में हमेशा सबसे बड़ा होता है।

<whisper>तो size order याद रखो: van der Waals radius metallic radius से बड़ा, जो covalent radius से बड़ा।</whisper> किसी noble gas के van der Waals radius को सीधे किसी neighbour के covalent radius से compare करना apples-to-oranges trap है।

अब canonical data, जिसका shape याद रखने लायक है। Period two के across, covalent radii picometres में: lithium one hundred fifty two, beryllium one hundred eleven, boron eighty eight, carbon seventy seven, nitrogen seventy four, oxygen sixty six, fluorine sixty four।

और group one में नीचे, picometres में: lithium one hundred fifty two, sodium one hundred eighty six, potassium two hundred thirty one, rubidium two hundred forty four, caesium two hundred sixty two। Period के across सिकुड़ते, group में नीचे बढ़ते - बिल्कुल जैसा engine predict करता है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Ionic radius: cations shrink, anions swell

board_events.text: Ionic radius: cations shrink, anions swell
Cation is smaller than the parent atom: electrons lost (often a whole shell), same $Z$ grips fewer electrons.
Example: a sodium atom 186 pm versus its cation 95 pm.
Anion is larger than the parent atom: added electrons raise repulsion, $Z_{\text{eff}}$ per electron drops.
Example: a fluorine atom 64 pm versus its anion 136 pm.
Isoelectronic species share the same electron count; among them, radius FALLS as $Z$ rises.
So for a fixed electron count, the only lever left is $Z$: more protons, tighter cloud, smaller ion.
This single rule decides most ordering questions

segments.text: Atoms become ions all the time in chemistry, so we need the size of ions too. Two clean rules cover it.
First, a cation is always smaller than its parent atom. When an atom loses electrons - often a whole outer shell - the same nuclear charge is now gripping fewer electrons, so the cloud contracts.
The numbers make it vivid: a sodium atom is about one hundred eighty six picometres, but the sodium cation is only about ninety five. Almost half the size.
Second, an anion is always larger than its parent atom. Adding electrons raises the mutual repulsion between them, and the effective nuclear charge felt per electron drops, so the cloud expands.
Again the numbers: a fluorine atom is about sixty four picometres, but the fluoride anion swells to about one hundred thirty six.

<whisper>Now the rule that quietly decides most exam orderings.</whisper> Isoelectronic species are atoms and ions that share the same electron count. Among them, radius falls as the nuclear charge Z rises.
The logic is simple. With the electron count fixed, the only variable left is Z. More protons pulling on the same-sized cloud means a tighter grip, and therefore a smaller ion.
That one rule - for equal electrons, higher Z means smaller - is what turns messy-looking ordering questions into a ten-second answer.
Chemistry में atoms हर वक़्त ions बनते हैं, तो हमें ions का size भी चाहिए। दो साफ rules इसे cover कर देते हैं।
पहला, cation हमेशा अपने parent atom से छोटा होता है। जब atom electrons खोता है - अक्सर पूरा outer shell - तो वही nuclear charge अब कम electrons को पकड़ रहा होता है, तो cloud contract हो जाता है।
Numbers इसे साफ कर देते हैं: sodium atom करीब one hundred eighty six picometres है, पर sodium cation सिर्फ करीब ninety five। लगभग आधा size।
दूसरा, anion हमेशा अपने parent atom से बड़ा होता है। Electrons जोड़ने से उनके बीच mutual repulsion बढ़ती है, और per electron महसूस होने वाला effective nuclear charge गिरता है, तो cloud फैल जाता है।
फिर से numbers: fluorine atom करीब sixty four picometres है, पर fluoride anion फूलकर करीब one hundred thirty six हो जाता है।

<whisper>अब वो rule जो चुपचाप ज़्यादातर exam orderings तय करता है।</whisper> Isoelectronic species वो atoms और ions हैं जिनका electron count same होता है। इनमें, radius गिरता है जैसे-जैसे nuclear charge Z बढ़ता है।
Logic simple है। Electron count fix होने पर, इकलौता बचा variable Z है। ज़्यादा protons उसी size के cloud को खींचें तो पकड़ tight, और इसलिए ion छोटा।
वही एक rule - equal electrons के लिए, ज़्यादा Z यानी छोटा - messy दिखने वाले ordering questions को दस सेकंड के answer में बदल देता है।

board_events.text: Ionisation enthalpy: definition and trend
The energy to remove the most loosely held electron from one mole of isolated gaseous atoms.
Always positive (endothermic). Successive values rise: $\Delta_i H_1 \lt \Delta_i H_2 \lt \Delta_i H_3$.
Each electron is torn from a more positive ion, so it costs more. Units: kJ per mol.
Trend: across a period IE rises (smaller, higher $Z_{\text{eff}}$); down a group IE falls (bigger, more shielding).
