board_events.text: Peaks at the noble gases He, Ne, Ar; deep troughs at the alkali metals Li, Na, K.

segments.text: Now to the quantity that measures how tightly an atom holds its electrons - the ionisation enthalpy.

It is defined as the energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from one mole of isolated, gaseous atoms. Notice every word: most loosely held, isolated, and gaseous - the definition is worth stating precisely in a board answer.
On the board, the first ionisation: a gaseous atom X becomes a gaseous cation X plus, releasing an electron, and the energy for this is delta i H one.

This energy is always positive - you must put energy in, so it is endothermic. And the successive values always climb: delta i H one is less than delta i H two, which is less than delta i H three, and so on.
Why do they climb? Because each electron is being torn from an increasingly positive ion, which grips harder. All of these are measured in kilojoules per mole.
Now the trend. Across a period, ionisation enthalpy generally rises - the atom is smaller with higher Z effective, so it grips tighter. Down a group it falls - the atom is bigger with more shielding.
<curious>Look at the graph of first ionisation enthalpy against atomic number, from one to twenty.</curious> It is not a smooth line - it is a sawtooth.

The peaks sit at the noble gases - helium, neon, argon - which cling to their electrons hardest. The deep troughs sit at the alkali metals - lithium, sodium, potassium - which give up their lone outer electron most easily.
अब उस quantity पर जो मापती है कि atom अपने electrons को कितनी tightly पकड़ता है - ionisation enthalpy।

इसे define किया जाता है उस energy के रूप में जो एक mole isolated, gaseous atoms में से सबसे loosely held electron हटाने के लिए चाहिए। हर शब्द ध्यान दो: most loosely held, isolated, और gaseous - board answer में इस definition को precisely लिखना फायदेमंद है।
Board पर, first ionisation: एक gaseous atom X बनता है gaseous cation X plus, एक electron छोड़ता है, और इसकी energy है delta i H one।
ये energy हमेशा positive होती है - आपको energy डालनी पड़ती है, तो ये endothermic है। और successive values हमेशा चढ़ती हैं: delta i H one, delta i H two से कम, जो delta i H three से कम, और आगे भी।
ये चढ़ती क्यों हैं? क्योंकि हर electron एक बढ़ते positive ion से खींचा जा रहा है, जो और ज़ोर से पकड़ता है। ये सब kilojoules per mole में मापे जाते हैं।
अब trend। Period के across, ionisation enthalpy आम तौर पर बढ़ती है - atom छोटा और Z effective ऊँचा, तो पकड़ tight। Group में नीचे ये गिरती है - atom बड़ा और shielding ज़्यादा।
<curious>First ionisation enthalpy बनाम atomic number का graph देखो, one से twenty तक।</curious> ये smooth line नहीं है - ये एक sawtooth है।

Peaks noble gases पर बैठते हैं - helium, neon, argon - जो अपने electrons को सबसे ज़ोर से पकड़ते हैं। गहरे troughs alkali metals पर - lithium, sodium, potassium - जो अपना अकेला outer electron सबसे आसानी से छोड़ देते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: The two celebrated ionisation-enthalpy reversals

board_events.text: The two celebrated IE reversals
Reversal 1 - Be greater than B: boron's outgoing electron sits in a higher-energy 2p orbital.
Beryllium's electron leaves a fully filled, stable $2s^{2}$ - harder to remove than boron's.
Reversal 2 - N greater than O: nitrogen has an exactly half-filled $2p^{3}$ set - symmetric and stable.
Oxygen's $2p^{4}$ forces a fourth electron to pair up, raising repulsion - so it leaves more easily.
A big jump between successive IEs signals the next electron comes from a noble-gas-like core.
The count of easy electrons before that jump equals the number of valence electrons - hence the group.
These dips recur in every period

segments.text: The sawtooth also has two little local dips that are favourite exam material - the two celebrated ionisation-enthalpy reversals in period two.

The first is that beryllium's ionisation enthalpy is greater than boron's - the reverse of the naive across-the-period rule. The reason: boron's outgoing electron sits in a higher-energy two p orbital.

Meanwhile beryllium's electron has to leave a fully filled, especially stable two s squared configuration. That extra stability makes beryllium's electron harder to remove than boron's - so beryllium wins.
The second reversal is that nitrogen's ionisation enthalpy is greater than oxygen's. Nitrogen has an exactly half-filled two p three set - a symmetric, low-repulsion, specially stable arrangement.

Oxygen, with two p four, is forced to pair a fourth electron into an already-occupied orbital, which raises the electron-electron repulsion. That paired electron leaves more easily - so oxygen's ionisation enthalpy actually dips below nitrogen's.

<whisper>Here is a bonus you can exploit in numerical questions.</whisper> A big jump between two successive ionisation energies signals that the next electron is being torn from a stable, noble-gas-like core.

And the number of easy electrons removed before that big jump equals the number of valence electrons - which immediately tells you the element's group. We will use exactly this in a worked example shortly.

The deep point: these dips are not one-off accidents of period two. Filled and half-filled subshell stability recurs in every period, so the same reversals reappear at magnesium versus aluminium, and at phosphorus versus sulphur.
इस sawtooth में दो छोटे local dips भी हैं जो favourite exam material हैं - period two के दो celebrated ionisation-enthalpy reversals।
पहला ये कि beryllium की ionisation enthalpy boron से ज़्यादा है - naive across-the-period rule का उल्टा। वजह: boron का बाहर जाने वाला electron एक higher-energy two p orbital में बैठा है।

जबकि beryllium के electron को एक fully filled, खास तौर पर stable two s squared configuration छोड़नी पड़ती है। वो extra stability beryllium के electron को boron के मुकाबले हटाना मुश्किल बना देती है - तो beryllium जीत जाता है।
दूसरा reversal ये कि nitrogen की ionisation enthalpy oxygen से ज़्यादा है। Nitrogen के पास exactly half-filled two p three set है - एक symmetric, low-repulsion, खास तौर पर stable arrangement।

Oxygen, two p four के साथ, एक चौथे electron को पहले से भरे orbital में pair करने पर मजबूर है, जिससे electron-electron repulsion बढ़ती है। वो paired electron आसानी से निकल जाता है - तो oxygen की ionisation enthalpy असल में nitrogen से नीचे गिर जाती है।

<whisper>यहाँ एक bonus है जिसे आप numerical questions में इस्तेमाल कर सकते हो।</whisper> दो successive ionisation energies के बीच बड़ा jump बताता है कि अगला electron एक stable, noble-gas-like core से खींचा जा रहा है।

और उस बड़े jump से पहले हटाए गए easy electrons की संख्या valence electrons की संख्या के बराबर होती है - जो तुरंत element का group बता देती है। ठीक इसी को हम थोड़ी देर में एक worked example में इस्तेमाल करेंगे।

गहरी बात: ये dips period two के one-off हादसे नहीं हैं। Filled और half-filled subshell stability हर period में दोहराती है, तो वही reversals magnesium बनाम aluminium, और phosphorus बनाम sulphur पर फिर से दिखते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Electron gain enthalpy and the F versus Cl surprise

board_events.text: Electron gain enthalpy and the F versus Cl surprise
The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms each gain an electron.
Usually negative (energy released); more negative means a stronger pull. Units: kJ per mol.
Trend: more negative across a period (smaller atoms pull harder); less negative down a group.
The surprise: chlorine releases MORE energy than fluorine on gaining an electron.
Fluorine's 2p sub-shell is so cramped that an incoming electron faces fierce repulsion in the tight n = 2 shell.
Chlorine's n = 3 shell is roomier, so its electron gain enthalpy is more negative than fluorine's.

segments.text: Next, the mirror-image quantity: instead of removing an electron, what happens when an atom gains one? That is the electron gain enthalpy.
It is the enthalpy change when one mole of isolated, gaseous atoms each gain an electron.
On the board: a gaseous atom X gains an electron to become the gaseous anion X minus, and the associated enthalpy is delta e g H.

This is usually negative, because energy is released when the atom accepts the electron. A more negative value means a stronger pull on the incoming electron. Again, the units are kilojoules per mole.

The trend follows the same engine: electron gain enthalpy becomes more negative across a period, since smaller atoms pull an incoming electron harder, and less negative down a group, since the new electron lands farther out.
<curious>But here is the single most-tested surprise in this whole subtopic.</curious> Chlorine releases more energy than fluorine on gaining an electron - even though fluorine sits above it.
The reason is size. Fluorine is so small that its two p sub-shell is already cramped, so an incoming electron faces fierce electron-electron repulsion in that tight n equals two shell.

Chlorine's n equals three shell is far roomier, the repulsion is milder, and so chlorine's electron gain enthalpy comes out more negative than fluorine's. Whenever both appear in a question, suspect this anomaly first.
अब mirror-image quantity: electron हटाने की बजाय, जब atom एक electron पाता है तो क्या होता है? वो है electron gain enthalpy।
ये वो enthalpy change है जब एक mole isolated, gaseous atoms में से हर एक एक electron पाता है।
Board पर: एक gaseous atom X एक electron पाकर gaseous anion X minus बनता है, और इससे जुड़ी enthalpy है delta e g H।

ये आम तौर पर negative होती है, क्योंकि atom के electron accept करने पर energy release होती है। ज़्यादा negative value का मतलब incoming electron पर ज़्यादा strong pull। फिर से, units kilojoules per mole हैं।

Trend वही engine follow करती है: period के across electron gain enthalpy ज़्यादा negative होती है, क्योंकि छोटे atoms incoming electron को ज़ोर से खींचते हैं, और group में नीचे कम negative, क्योंकि नया electron दूर जा गिरता है।
<curious>पर यहाँ इस पूरे subtopic का सबसे ज़्यादा test होने वाला surprise है।</curious> Chlorine, fluorine से ज़्यादा energy release करता है electron पाने पर - भले fluorine उसके ऊपर बैठा हो।
वजह size है। Fluorine इतना छोटा है कि उसका two p sub-shell पहले से cramped है, तो incoming electron को उस tight n बराबर two shell में fierce electron-electron repulsion झेलनी पड़ती है।

Chlorine का n बराबर three shell कहीं ज़्यादा roomy है, repulsion milder है, और इसलिए chlorine की electron gain enthalpy fluorine से ज़्यादा negative निकलती है। जब भी दोनों किसी question में दिखें, पहले इस anomaly पर शक करो।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Electronegativity: one idea, three scales

board_events.text: Electronegativity: one idea, three scales
The tendency of a bonded atom to attract the shared electron pair towards itself. It is dimensionless.
Pauling scale (most used): fluorine set at 4.0 as the maximum; derived from bond energies.
Allred-Rochow treats EN as the electrostatic pull on a peripheral electron.
All scales agree on the trend: EN rises across a period, falls down a group. Highest F, lowest Cs.
Same engine as IE: small size + high $Z_{\text{eff}}$ means a strong pull on shared electrons.

segments.text: The last physical property in this subtopic is electronegativity - and it ties everything together.

Electronegativity is the tendency of a bonded atom to attract the shared electron pair towards itself. Unlike ionisation enthalpy or electron gain enthalpy, it is dimensionless - a relative number, not something you measure directly. There are three common scales.
The Pauling scale is the one you will use most. It is derived from bond energies, and it fixes fluorine at four point zero as the maximum, with every other element scaled below that.

The Mulliken scale takes a different route: it defines electronegativity as the average of the ionisation energy and the electron affinity. Mulliken values run about two point eight times the Pauling values, so you convert by dividing the Mulliken value by two point eight.
The Allred-Rochow scale takes yet another view - it treats electronegativity as the electrostatic force pulling on a peripheral electron.
Its formula puts that force together: chi A R equals zero point three five nine times Z effective over r squared, plus zero point seven four four, with r the covalent radius.

<excited>But here is the reassuring part.</excited> All three scales, however they compute the number, agree completely on the trend: electronegativity rises across a period and falls down a group, with fluorine highest and caesium lowest.

And notice it is the very same engine as ionisation enthalpy: small size plus high Z effective means a strong pull on the shared electrons - so electronegativity mirrors the ionisation-enthalpy trend almost exactly.
इस subtopic की आखिरी physical property है electronegativity - और ये सब कुछ आपस में बाँध देती है।

Electronegativity एक bonded atom की वो tendency है कि shared electron pair को अपनी तरफ खींचे। Ionisation enthalpy या electron gain enthalpy के उलट, ये dimensionless है - एक relative number, जिसे आप सीधे measure नहीं करते। इसके तीन common scales हैं।
Pauling scale वो है जो आप सबसे ज़्यादा use करोगे। ये bond energies से derive होती है, और fluorine को four point zero पर maximum के रूप में fix करती है, बाकी हर element उसके नीचे scale होता है।

Mulliken scale अलग रास्ता लेती है: ये electronegativity को ionisation energy और electron affinity की average के रूप में define करती है। Mulliken values Pauling values की करीब two point eight गुना होती हैं, तो आप Mulliken value को two point eight से divide करके convert करते हो।
Allred-Rochow scale एक और नज़रिया लेती है - ये electronegativity को एक peripheral electron पर लगने वाली electrostatic force मानती है।
इसका formula उस force को जोड़ता है: chi A R बराबर zero point three five nine गुना Z effective बटा r squared, plus zero point seven four four, जहाँ r covalent radius है।

<excited>पर यहाँ राहत की बात है।</excited> तीनों scales, चाहे number कैसे भी compute करें, trend पर पूरी तरह सहमत हैं: electronegativity period के across बढ़ती है और group में नीचे गिरती है, fluorine सबसे ऊँचा और caesium सबसे नीचा।

और ध्यान दो ये वही engine है जो ionisation enthalpy का है: छोटा size plus ऊँचा Z effective यानी shared electrons पर strong pull - तो electronegativity ionisation-enthalpy trend को लगभग हूबहू mirror करती है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: The d- and f-screening anomaly

board_events.text: The d- and f-screening anomaly
Going down group 13 you expect each element larger - yet gallium is slightly SMALLER than aluminium.
Between Al and Ga sit ten 3d electrons (first appearing after Al) that screen poorly.
The extra nuclear charge is incompletely cancelled, so gallium is contracted below aluminium.
The same poor d-screening makes group-13 ionisation energies fall irregularly, not smoothly.
The observed order is B greater than Tl greater than Ga, then Al, then In.
Lower down, poor f-screening (the lanthanoid contraction) pushes In and Tl to nearly equal size.
Why this matters: not every trend is smooth

segments.text: Before the formulas, one honest complication: the trends are general, not absolute. The clearest example is the d and f screening anomaly in group thirteen.
Going straight down group thirteen, you would confidently expect each element to be larger than the one above. Yet gallium comes out slightly smaller than aluminium - a genuine surprise.
<curious>The culprit sits right between them.</curious> Between aluminium and gallium, ten three d electrons appear for the first time, and d electrons are poor at shielding.

Because that d shell screens so weakly, the extra nuclear charge added across the transition series is only incompletely cancelled. The valence electrons of gallium feel a higher effective pull than expected, and gallium is contracted right down below aluminium.
The same poor d-screening also shows up in ionisation energy. Down group thirteen the first ionisation energies do not fall smoothly - they wobble.
The observed order is boron greatest, then thallium, then gallium, then aluminium, then indium - clearly not the tidy top-to-bottom decrease you would first guess.

And lower down, the poor screening by f electrons - the lanthanoid contraction - is what pushes indium and thallium to nearly the same size. That deeper story belongs to Class twelve, but the fingerprint appears here.

The reason this matters is simple: do not assume every trend is a smooth slope. Wherever poorly-shielding d or f electrons appear, the trend develops a kink - and examiners aim straight at those kinks.
Formulas से पहले, एक ईमानदार complication: trends general हैं, absolute नहीं। सबसे साफ example है group thirteen में d और f screening anomaly।
Group thirteen में सीधे नीचे जाते हुए, आप confidently expect करोगे कि हर element ऊपर वाले से बड़ा हो। पर gallium aluminium से थोड़ा छोटा निकलता है - एक असली surprise।
<curious>Culprit ठीक उन्हीं के बीच बैठा है।</curious> Aluminium और gallium के बीच, दस three d electrons पहली बार आते हैं, और d electrons shielding में कमज़ोर होते हैं।

क्योंकि वो d shell इतना weakly screen करता है, transition series के across जुड़ी extra nuclear charge सिर्फ incompletely cancel होती है। Gallium के valence electrons expected से ऊँचा effective pull महसूस करते हैं, और gallium सिकुड़कर aluminium के नीचे आ जाता है।
वही poor d-screening ionisation energy में भी दिखता है। Group thirteen में नीचे first ionisation energies smoothly नहीं गिरतीं - वो डगमगाती हैं।
Observed order है boron सबसे ज़्यादा, फिर thallium, फिर gallium, फिर aluminium, फिर indium - साफ तौर पर वो tidy top-to-bottom decrease नहीं जो आप पहले सोचोगे।
और नीचे, f electrons का poor screening - lanthanoid contraction - वो indium और thallium को लगभग एक ही size पर धकेल देता है। वो गहरी कहानी Class twelve की है, पर उसका fingerprint यहाँ दिखता है।

ये matter क्यों करता है, simple है: ये मत मानो कि हर trend एक smooth slope है। जहाँ भी poorly-shielding d या f electrons आते हैं, trend में एक kink बन जाता है - और examiners सीधे उन kinks पर निशाना लगाते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Physical-property toolkit

board_events.text: Physical-property toolkit
The master engine: across a period $Z_{\text{eff}}$ rises; down a group distance and shielding win.

board_events.latex: X(g) \rightarrow X^{+}(g) + e^{-}\ \ \Delta_i H_1 \qquad X^{+}(g) \rightarrow X^{2+}(g) + e^{-}\ \ \Delta_i H_2

board_events.text: Successive values climb: $\Delta_i H_1 \lt \Delta_i H_2 \lt \Delta_i H_3$.

segments.text: Let's gather this subtopic's working formulas in one place - your physical-property toolkit for the exam.
At the top, the master engine: effective nuclear charge equals Z minus sigma - the true nuclear charge minus the inner-electron screening.
Keep its behaviour attached: across a period Z effective rises, so atoms shrink and grip tighter; down a group, distance and shielding win, so atoms grow.
For size, the covalent radius is half the internuclear distance between two like bonded atoms, and the fixed size order is van der Waals greater than metallic greater than covalent.
For ionisation, the first step turns a gaseous atom into its plus-one cation with energy delta i H one, and the second step turns that into the plus-two cation with delta i H two.
And remember, those successive values always climb - delta i H one less than delta i H two less than delta i H three - because each electron leaves a more positive ion.
For electron gain, a gaseous atom takes an electron to become the minus-one anion, with enthalpy delta e g H, usually negative.
For electronegativity, the Mulliken value is the average of ionisation energy and electron affinity, and you convert to the Pauling scale by dividing by two point eight.

And the Allred-Rochow scale writes electronegativity as zero point three five nine times Z effective over radius squared, plus zero point seven four four. Keep this whole panel in view and every trend question becomes a lookup, not a struggle.
चलो इस subtopic के काम आने वाले formulas एक जगह इकट्ठा करते हैं - exam के लिए आपका physical-property toolkit।
सबसे ऊपर, master engine: effective nuclear charge बराबर Z minus sigma - असली nuclear charge minus inner-electron screening।
इसका behaviour साथ जोड़े रखो: period के across Z effective बढ़ता है, तो atoms सिकुड़ते और tight पकड़ते हैं; group में नीचे, distance और shielding जीतते हैं, तो atoms बढ़ते हैं।
Size के लिए, covalent radius दो like bonded atoms के बीच की internuclear distance का आधा है, और fixed size order है van der Waals, metallic से बड़ा, जो covalent से बड़ा।
Ionisation के लिए, पहला step एक gaseous atom को उसके plus-one cation में बदलता है energy delta i H one के साथ, और दूसरा step उसे plus-two cation में delta i H two के साथ।
और याद रखो, वो successive values हमेशा चढ़ती हैं - delta i H one, delta i H two से कम, जो delta i H three से कम - क्योंकि हर electron एक ज़्यादा positive ion छोड़ता है।
Electron gain के लिए, एक gaseous atom एक electron लेकर minus-one anion बनता है, enthalpy delta e g H के साथ, आम तौर पर negative।
Electronegativity के लिए, Mulliken value ionisation energy और electron affinity की average है, और आप Pauling scale पर two point eight से divide करके convert करते हो।

<excited>और Allred-Rochow scale electronegativity को zero point three five nine गुना Z effective बटा radius squared, plus zero point seven four four लिखती है।</excited> इस पूरे panel को नज़र में रखो और हर trend question struggle की बजाय एक lookup बन जाता है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Worked example: order isoelectronic species by radius

board_events.text: Worked Example: order isoelectronic species by radius
Arrange by increasing ionic radius: $Al^{3+}, Mg^{2+}, Na^{+}, F^{-}, O^{2-}$.
All five have 10 electrons - they are isoelectronic (neon-like).
Rule: for isoelectronic species, radius decreases as nuclear charge $Z$ increases.
Nuclear charges: $O$ 8, $F$ 9, $Na$ 11, $Mg$ 12, $Al$ 13.
Higher $Z$ grips the same 10 electrons tighter, so the highest-charge cation is smallest.
Increasing radius: $Al^{3+} \lt Mg^{2+} \lt Na^{+} \lt F^{-} \lt O^{2-}$.
One rule, instant ordering

segments.text: Let's use the isoelectronic rule on a classic C B S E ordering question.
We are asked to arrange five species by increasing ionic radius: the aluminium three plus ion, magnesium two plus, sodium plus, fluoride minus, and oxide two minus.

The first move is to count electrons. Aluminium three plus has lost three from thirteen, leaving ten. Do the same for each and every one lands on ten electrons - they are all isoelectronic, with a neon-like configuration.
Now the rule we built: for an isoelectronic set, radius decreases as the nuclear charge Z increases. Electron count is fixed, so Z is the only lever.
List the nuclear charges: oxygen eight, fluorine nine, sodium eleven, magnesium twelve, aluminium thirteen.
Higher Z pulls the same ten electrons in more tightly, so the species with the largest nuclear charge is the smallest ion, and the one with the smallest nuclear charge is the largest.
<excited>So increasing radius runs: aluminium three plus, then magnesium two plus, then sodium plus, then fluoride minus, then oxide two minus as the largest.</excited>
One rule, ordered in seconds. The trap to avoid is ranking by the charge sign or by group position - only nuclear charge matters here.
चलो isoelectronic rule को एक classic C B S E ordering question पर इस्तेमाल करते हैं।
हमें पाँच species को increasing ionic radius से arrange करना है: aluminium three plus ion, magnesium two plus, sodium plus, fluoride minus, और oxide two minus।
पहला कदम electrons गिनना है। Aluminium three plus ने तेरह में से तीन खोए, बचे दस। हर एक के लिए यही करो और सब दस electrons पर आ जाते हैं - ये सब isoelectronic हैं, neon-like configuration के साथ।
अब वो rule जो हमने बनाया: isoelectronic set के लिए, radius घटता है जैसे-जैसे nuclear charge Z बढ़ता है। Electron count fix है, तो Z ही इकलौता lever है।
Nuclear charges list करो: oxygen eight, fluorine nine, sodium eleven, magnesium twelve, aluminium thirteen।
ज़्यादा Z उन्हीं दस electrons को ज़्यादा tightly खींचता है, तो सबसे बड़ी nuclear charge वाली species सबसे छोटा ion है, और सबसे छोटी nuclear charge वाली सबसे बड़ा।
<excited>तो increasing radius चलता है: aluminium three plus, फिर magnesium two plus, फिर sodium plus, फिर fluoride minus, फिर oxide two minus सबसे बड़ा।</excited>
एक rule, सेकंडों में order। बचने वाला trap है charge sign या group position से rank करना - यहाँ सिर्फ nuclear charge matter करता है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Worked example: most negative electron gain enthalpy?

board_events.text: Worked Example: most negative electron gain enthalpy?
Which has the most negative electron gain enthalpy: S, Cl, F, or P?
Instinct picks F (topmost halogen) - that is the trap.
Across period 3 (P to S to Cl): EGE grows more negative, so Cl beats S beats P.
Now Cl versus F: F's tiny 2p shell over-repels the incoming electron.
So the winner is chlorine, not fluorine.
Whenever F and Cl both appear, suspect the small-shell repulsion anomaly first.
The single most-tested EGE fact in NEET

segments.text: This is a N E E T speed trap on electron gain enthalpy - and it is designed to catch a reflex.
The question: which of sulphur, chlorine, fluorine, and phosphorus has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?
<curious>The instinct is to say fluorine - it is the topmost halogen, so surely it grabs electrons hardest.</curious> That instinct is exactly the trap.
Work it in two moves. First, across period three, from phosphorus to sulphur to chlorine, electron gain enthalpy grows more negative - so chlorine beats sulphur, which beats phosphorus.
Now the real contest, chlorine versus fluorine. Fluorine's two p shell is so tiny and cramped that an incoming electron is strongly repelled by the electrons already there.
So the winner is chlorine, not fluorine - chlorine's roomier three shell lets the new electron settle with far less repulsion, giving a more negative value.
The takeaway is a habit: whenever fluorine and chlorine both appear in an electron-gain question, suspect this small-shell repulsion anomaly before you answer.
This is the single most-tested electron gain enthalpy fact in N E E T - so it is worth locking in permanently.
ये electron gain enthalpy पर एक N E E T speed trap है - और ये एक reflex को पकड़ने के लिए बना है।
सवाल: sulphur, chlorine, fluorine, और phosphorus में से किसकी electron gain enthalpy सबसे ज़्यादा negative है?
<curious>Instinct कहता है fluorine - ये सबसे ऊपर वाला halogen है, तो ज़रूर electrons सबसे ज़ोर से पकड़ेगा।</curious> वही instinct exact trap है।
इसे दो चालों में करो। पहले, period three के across, phosphorus से sulphur से chlorine तक, electron gain enthalpy ज़्यादा negative होती जाती है - तो chlorine sulphur से आगे, जो phosphorus से आगे।
अब असली मुक़ाबला, chlorine बनाम fluorine। Fluorine का two p shell इतना छोटा और cramped है कि incoming electron को वहाँ पहले से मौजूद electrons strongly repel करते हैं।
तो winner है chlorine, fluorine नहीं - chlorine का ज़्यादा roomy three shell नए electron को कहीं कम repulsion के साथ settle होने देता है, जिससे value ज़्यादा negative।
Takeaway एक आदत है: जब भी fluorine और chlorine दोनों किसी electron-gain question में दिखें, answer देने से पहले इस small-shell repulsion anomaly पर शक करो।
ये N E E T में electron gain enthalpy का सबसे ज़्यादा test होने वाला fact है - तो इसे हमेशा के लिए lock कर लेना फायदेमंद है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Worked example: read the IE jumps to find the group

board_events.text: Worked Example: read the IE jumps to find the group
First four ionisation enthalpies of Q (kJ per mol): 736, 1448, 7720, 10560.
(a) How many valence electrons? Inspect the jumps between successive values.
Modest 736 to 1448, then a fivefold leap 1448 to 7720 - the 3rd electron comes from a stable core.
So Q has 2 valence electrons.
(b) Two easily removed electrons means Group 2 (alkaline earth), valence configuration $ns^{2}$.
(c) A group-2 element forms a +2 ion, combining 1:1 with $O^{2-}$, giving oxide formula QO.
Biggest ratio jump: electrons before it equal the group

segments.text: Now a J E E Main level question that turns the ionisation-jump idea into a full answer. We are given the first four ionisation enthalpies of an element Q, in kilojoules per mole: seven thirty six, fourteen forty eight, seven thousand seven twenty, and ten thousand five sixty.
Part a asks how many valence electrons Q has, and the method is to inspect the jumps between successive values.
Look at the gaps. From seven thirty six to fourteen forty eight is a modest rise. But from fourteen forty eight to seven thousand seven twenty is more than a fivefold leap - a huge jump.

<whisper>That huge jump is the tell.</whisper> It means the third electron is being torn from a stable, noble-gas-like core, which is far harder to disturb. So only the first two electrons came off easily.
Therefore Q has exactly two valence electrons.
Part b follows immediately. Two easily removed electrons means Q is in group two, the alkaline earth metals, with a valence configuration of n s two.
Part c: a group-two element forms a plus-two ion, and it combines one-to-one with the oxide ion, oxygen two minus. So the formula of its most stable oxide is Q O.

The general skill: find the biggest ratio jump between successive ionisation energies, and the number of electrons removed before that jump equals the group number. That one move stitches trend, configuration, and chemistry together.

अब एक J E E Main level question जो ionisation-jump idea को पूरे answer में बदल देता है। हमें एक element Q की पहली चार ionisation enthalpies दी हैं, kilojoules per mole में: seven thirty six, fourteen forty eight, seven thousand seven twenty, और ten thousand five sixty।
Part a पूछता है कि Q के कितने valence electrons हैं, और तरीका है successive values के बीच के jumps को inspect करना।
Gaps देखो। Seven thirty six से fourteen forty eight तक modest rise। पर fourteen forty eight से seven thousand seven twenty तक fivefold से ज़्यादा leap - एक बड़ा jump।
<whisper>वो बड़ा jump ही इशारा है।</whisper> इसका मतलब तीसरा electron एक stable, noble-gas-like core से खींचा जा रहा है, जिसे disturb करना कहीं मुश्किल है। तो सिर्फ पहले दो electrons आसानी से निकले।
इसलिए Q के ठीक दो valence electrons हैं।
Part b तुरंत निकलता है। दो आसानी से निकलने वाले electrons का मतलब Q group two में है, alkaline earth metals, valence configuration n s two के साथ।
Part c: एक group-two element plus-two ion बनाता है, और oxide ion, oxygen two minus, के साथ one-to-one combine करता है। तो इसके most stable oxide का formula है Q O।

General skill: successive ionisation energies के बीच सबसे बड़ा ratio jump ढूँढ़ो, और उस jump से पहले निकले electrons की संख्या group number के बराबर होती है। वो एक चाल trend, configuration, और chemistry को एक साथ जोड़ देती है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Worked example: locate and predict the IE reversals

board_events.text: Worked Example: locate and predict the IE reversals
Observed period-2 order: Li less than B less than Be less than C less than O less than N less than F less than Ne.
(a) Two reversals break the simple increase-across-a-period rule.
Be greater than B: Be's electron leaves a filled, stable $2s^{2}$; B's leaves a higher $2p^{1}$.
N greater than O: N's $2p^{3}$ is half-filled and stable; O's $2p^{4}$ has extra pairing repulsion.
(b) Predict period 3: filled-s versus $p^{1}$ recurs at Mg versus Al, so expect Mg greater than Al.
Half-filled $p^{3}$ recurs at P versus S, so expect P greater than S. Both are observed.
The reversal is structural, not a coincidence

segments.text: We close the examples with a J E E Advanced question that generalises the two reversals. The observed period-two order of first ionisation enthalpy is: lithium, then boron, then beryllium, then carbon, then oxygen, then nitrogen, then fluorine, then neon.
Read that order carefully and you will see it is mostly increasing, but with two spots where it reverses the simple across-the-period rule.
Part a asks us to identify and explain those two reversals.

The first is beryllium above boron. Beryllium's outgoing electron leaves a filled, stable two s squared configuration, whereas boron's leaves a higher-energy, less stable two p one. So boron's electron is easier to remove - and beryllium's ionisation enthalpy sits higher.

The second is nitrogen above oxygen. Nitrogen's two p three is exactly half-filled - symmetric and stable - while oxygen's two p four carries one paired electron with extra repulsion, which comes off more easily. So nitrogen's ionisation enthalpy sits higher.

<curious>Now part b - can we predict the same in period three?</curious> The filled-s versus p-one situation recurs at magnesium versus aluminium, so we expect magnesium's ionisation enthalpy to exceed aluminium's.
And the half-filled p-three situation recurs at phosphorus versus sulphur, so we expect phosphorus to exceed sulphur. Both predictions are, in fact, observed experimentally.

That is the real lesson: these reversals are structural, not coincidences. Wherever a period crosses from a filled s to a p one, or from a half-filled p three to a p four, the ionisation enthalpy dips against the naive trend - every single time.

हम examples को एक J E E Advanced question से बंद करते हैं जो दोनों reversals को generalise करता है। First ionisation enthalpy का observed period-two order है: lithium, फिर boron, फिर beryllium, फिर carbon, फिर oxygen, फिर nitrogen, फिर fluorine, फिर neon।
उस order को ध्यान से पढ़ो और दिखेगा कि ये ज़्यादातर increasing है, पर दो जगह जहाँ ये simple across-the-period rule को reverse करता है।
Part a कहता है उन दो reversals को identify और explain करो।

पहला है beryllium, boron के ऊपर। Beryllium का बाहर जाने वाला electron एक filled, stable two s squared configuration छोड़ता है, जबकि boron का एक higher-energy, कम stable two p one। तो boron का electron हटाना आसान - और beryllium की ionisation enthalpy ऊँची बैठती है।

दूसरा है nitrogen, oxygen के ऊपर। Nitrogen का two p three exactly half-filled है - symmetric और stable - जबकि oxygen का two p four एक paired electron रखता है extra repulsion के साथ, जो आसानी से निकल जाता है। तो nitrogen की ionisation enthalpy ऊँची बैठती है।

<curious>अब part b - क्या हम period three में यही predict कर सकते हैं?</curious> Filled-s बनाम p-one situation magnesium बनाम aluminium पर दोहराती है, तो हम expect करते हैं magnesium की ionisation enthalpy aluminium से ज़्यादा हो।
और half-filled p-three situation phosphorus बनाम sulphur पर दोहराती है, तो हम expect करते हैं phosphorus, sulphur से ज़्यादा हो। दोनों predictions असल में experimentally observed हैं।

यही असली lesson है: ये reversals structural हैं, coincidence नहीं। जहाँ भी period एक filled s से p one में, या half-filled p three से p four में जाता है, ionisation enthalpy naive trend के खिलाफ dip करती है - हर एक बार।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Common pitfalls and pro-tips
Pitfall 1: ordering isoelectronic species wrong. Equal electrons means only $Z$ matters; bigger $Z$ = smaller ion.
Pitfall 2: assuming fluorine has the most negative EGE. It is chlorine - F's tiny 2p over-repels.
Pitfall 3: forgetting the two IE reversals at filled-s (Be, Mg) and half-filled-p (N, P).
Pitfall 4: mixing units. EN and metallic character are unitless; IE and EGE are in kJ per mol.
Master arrow: across a period $Z_{\text{eff}}$ up, size down; IE up, EGE more negative, EN up. Down a group, reverse.
Then memorise four exception flags: Be/Mg, N/P (IE dips), F vs Cl (EGE), Ga smaller than Al (size/IE).
For successive-IE questions, find the biggest ratio jump; electrons before it equal the group number.

segments.text: Let's close the subtopic by collecting the traps and the shortcuts.

<whisper>Pitfall one: ordering isoelectronic species the wrong way.</whisper> With equal electrons only the nuclear charge matters - a bigger Z means a smaller ion. Do not order by charge sign or by group position.
Pitfall two: assuming fluorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy. It is chlorine - fluorine's tiny two p shell over-repels the incoming electron. Whenever both appear, check for this.

Pitfall three: forgetting the two ionisation-enthalpy reversals. It is wrong to say ionisation enthalpy always increases across a period - it dips at the filled-s points, beryllium and magnesium, and the half-filled-p points, nitrogen and phosphorus.
Pitfall four: mixing up units. Electronegativity and metallic character are unitless; ionisation enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy are measured in kilojoules per mole.

Now the master pro-tip - reduce the whole subtopic to one arrow. Across a period, Z effective goes up and size goes down, and everything else follows: ionisation enthalpy up, electron gain enthalpy more negative, electronegativity up. Down a group, every one of those reverses.

Then memorise just four exception flags: beryllium and magnesium, nitrogen and phosphorus for the ionisation dips, fluorine versus chlorine for electron gain enthalpy, and gallium being smaller than aluminium for size and ionisation energy. If a question is not flagged, trust the arrow and move on.

And for successive-ionisation questions, always find the biggest ratio jump - the number of electrons removed before that jump is the group number. That single move answers a whole family of J E E questions.
चलो subtopic को traps और shortcuts इकट्ठा करके बंद करते हैं।

<whisper>Pitfall one: isoelectronic species को गलत तरीके से order करना।</whisper> Equal electrons पर सिर्फ nuclear charge matter करता है - ज़्यादा Z यानी छोटा ion। Charge sign या group position से order मत करो।
Pitfall two: मान लेना कि fluorine की electron gain enthalpy सबसे negative है। वो chlorine है - fluorine का छोटा two p shell incoming electron को over-repel करता है। जब भी दोनों दिखें, इसे check करो।

Pitfall three: दो ionisation-enthalpy reversals भूल जाना। ये कहना गलत है कि ionisation enthalpy period के across हमेशा बढ़ती है - ये filled-s points, beryllium और magnesium, और half-filled-p points, nitrogen और phosphorus पर dip करती है।
Pitfall four: units मिलाना। Electronegativity और metallic character unitless हैं; ionisation enthalpy और electron gain enthalpy kilojoules per mole में मापे जाते हैं।

अब master pro-tip - पूरे subtopic को एक arrow में समेट दो। Period के across, Z effective ऊपर और size नीचे, और बाकी सब follow करता है: ionisation enthalpy up, electron gain enthalpy more negative, electronegativity up। Group में नीचे, इनमें से हर एक reverse।

फिर बस चार exception flags याद करो: beryllium और magnesium, nitrogen और phosphorus ionisation dips के लिए, fluorine बनाम chlorine electron gain enthalpy के लिए, और gallium का aluminium से छोटा होना size और ionisation energy के लिए। अगर question flagged नहीं है, arrow पर भरोसा करो और आगे बढ़ो।

और successive-ionisation questions के लिए, हमेशा सबसे बड़ा ratio jump ढूँढ़ो - उस jump से पहले निकले electrons की संख्या group number है। वो एक चाल J E E questions के पूरे परिवार को answer कर देती है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Chemistry is electronic configuration in disguise

board_events.text: Chemistry is electronic configuration in disguise
Every chemical property is just the valence-shell configuration wearing a different costume.
Think of an atom's outer electrons as the cash a shopkeeper keeps in the front drawer.
Valence, the combining capacity, is how many deals that cash can fund.
Group 1 carries one loose note ($ns^{1}$) - hands it over and becomes +1. Group 17 is one note short ($ns^{2}np^{5}$) - grabs one and becomes -1.
The drawer fills steadily across a period, so combining capacity rises then falls in a predictable rhythm.
This subtopic asks the payoff: how do physical trends become how an element actually reacts and combines?
Bridge from physical trends to real reactions

segments.text: In the last subtopic we tracked the physical trends - size, ionisation energy, electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity. Now comes the payoff question: how do those trends translate into how an element actually reacts and combines?

<curious>The bridge is one idea you have already met.</curious> Every chemical property is just the valence-shell electronic configuration wearing a different costume. Nothing new is being introduced - the same outer electrons are simply doing chemistry now.
Here is the picture to hold. Think of an element's outer electrons as the cash a shopkeeper keeps in the front drawer of the shop.
The valence - the combining capacity - is simply how many deals that front-drawer cash can fund. It is the number of bonds the atom can strike.

A group-one metal carries a single loose note, its n s one electron. It hands that note over instantly and becomes plus one. A group-seventeen element is one note short of a full drawer, n s two n p five, so it grabs one and becomes minus one.
And the drawer fills up steadily as you cross a period. So the combining capacity rises and then falls in a predictable rhythm - which is the pattern we will pin down next.
So the whole subtopic is really one question: how do the physical trends from before turn into real reactivity, real formulae, real oxides?
That is the bridge - from the physical trends of Sub-two to the actual chemistry of how elements combine. Keep the drawer picture in mind; everything else hangs off it.

पिछले subtopic में हमने physical trends track कीं - size, ionisation energy, electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity। अब payoff सवाल आता है: वो trends इसमें कैसे बदलती हैं कि element असल में कैसे react और combine करता है?

<curious>Bridge एक ऐसा idea है जिससे आप पहले मिल चुके हो।</curious> हर chemical property बस valence-shell electronic configuration है जो एक अलग costume पहने हुए है। कुछ नया नहीं आ रहा - वही outer electrons अब chemistry कर रहे हैं।
ये तस्वीर पकड़े रखो। Element के outer electrons को वो cash समझो जो एक shopkeeper दुकान के front drawer में रखता है।
Valence - combining capacity - बस ये है कि उस front-drawer की cash कितने deals fund कर सकती है। ये उन bonds की संख्या है जो atom बना सकता है।

एक group-one metal एक अकेला loose note रखता है, उसका n s one electron। वो note तुरंत दे देता है और plus one बन जाता है। एक group-seventeen element एक note से drawer भरने में कम है, n s two n p five, तो वो एक grab करके minus one बन जाता है।
और drawer steadily भरता है जैसे-जैसे आप period cross करते हो। तो combining capacity एक predictable rhythm में बढ़ती है फिर गिरती है - यही pattern हम आगे pin down करेंगे।
तो पूरा subtopic असल में एक सवाल है: पहले की physical trends कैसे बदलती हैं असली reactivity, असली formulae, असली oxides में?
यही bridge है - Sub-two की physical trends से लेकर elements कैसे combine करते हैं उसकी असली chemistry तक। Drawer वाली तस्वीर याद रखो; बाकी सब उसी पर टिका है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Reactivity peaks at both ends of a period

board_events.text: Reactivity: high at both ends, low in the middle
Picture a tug-of-war across a period.
Far left: alkali metals, desperate to let go of one rope-end - wildly reactive reducing agents.
Far right: halogens, desperate to grab a rope - wildly reactive oxidising agents.
Middle (carbon, silicon): balanced players who neither give nor grab - the least reactive.
So reactivity is high at both ends of a period and lowest in the centre - mirroring the IE and EGE extremes.
Left to right, elements shift metallic (basic oxides) to metalloid to non-metallic (acidic oxides).
$Na_2O$ is strongly basic; $Cl_2O_7$ strongly acidic; $Al_2O_3$ sits between as amphoteric.

segments.text: Now let's turn the drawer picture into reactivity, using a tournament image.
Picture a tug-of-war tournament laid out across a period, left to right.
On the far left stand the alkali metals. They are desperate to let go of their single rope-end - to lose one electron - so they are wildly reactive, acting as powerful reducing agents.
On the far right stand the halogens. They are desperate to grab a rope - to gain an electron - so they too are wildly reactive, acting as powerful oxidising agents.
<excited>And in the middle sit the balanced players - carbon and silicon - who neither give nor grab easily.</excited> They are the least reactive of the lot.
So chemical reactivity is high at both ends of a period and lowest in the centre - which mirrors exactly the ionisation-energy and electron-gain-enthalpy extremes we found in the last subtopic.

A second pattern rides along with it. Moving left to right, elements shift from metallic - the electron-givers that form basic oxides - through the metalloids, to non-metallic - the electron-grabbers that form acidic oxides.

You can see it in the oxides directly. Sodium's oxide is strongly basic; chlorine's highest oxide is strongly acidic; and aluminium's oxide sits right in between as amphoteric - reacting with both acids and bases.
अब drawer वाली तस्वीर को reactivity में बदलते हैं, एक tournament image से।
एक tug-of-war tournament imagine करो जो period के across बिछा है, left to right।
सबसे बाईं ओर alkali metals खड़े हैं। वो अपना अकेला rope-end छोड़ने को बेताब हैं - एक electron खोने को - तो वो wildly reactive हैं, powerful reducing agents की तरह।
सबसे दाईं ओर halogens खड़े हैं। वो एक rope grab करने को बेताब हैं - एक electron पाने को - तो वो भी wildly reactive हैं, powerful oxidising agents की तरह।
<excited>और बीच में balanced players बैठे हैं - carbon और silicon - जो न आसानी से देते हैं न grab करते हैं।</excited> वो पूरी lot में सबसे कम reactive हैं।
तो chemical reactivity period के दोनों सिरों पर high है और बीच में सबसे low - जो बिल्कुल उन ionisation-energy और electron-gain-enthalpy extremes को mirror करती है जो हमें पिछले subtopic में मिले।

इसके साथ एक दूसरा pattern भी चलता है। Left to right जाते हुए, elements metallic - electron-givers जो basic oxides बनाते हैं - से होते हुए metalloids से, non-metallic - electron-grabbers जो acidic oxides बनाते हैं - में shift होते हैं।

ये आप oxides में सीधे देख सकते हो। Sodium का oxide strongly basic है; chlorine का highest oxide strongly acidic; और aluminium का oxide ठीक बीच में amphoteric बैठता है - acids और bases दोनों से react करता हुआ।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Valence: the N or 8 minus N rule

board_events.text: Valence: the N or 8 minus N rule
For representative elements: valence = (number of valence electrons) or (8 minus that number), whichever reaches the octet.
Group number (old A-convention, $s/p$ block) equals the number of valence electrons.
Period-3 valence with respect to oxygen climbs: Na 1, Mg 2, Al 3, Si 4, P 5, S 6, Cl 7.
Matching oxides: $Na_2O, MgO, Al_2O_3, SiO_2, P_2O_5, SO_3, Cl_2O_7$.
Valence with respect to hydrogen rises then falls: 1, 2, 3, 4, then 3, 2, 1.
Matching hydrides: $NaH, MgH_2, AlH_3, SiH_4, PH_3, H_2S, HCl$.
So the oxygen scale climbs 1 to 7; the hydrogen scale rises 1 to 4 then falls back to 1.

segments.text: Let's pin down valence precisely - the single most useful number for predicting formulae.
For the representative elements, valence equals either the number of valence electrons, or eight minus that number - whichever route reaches a noble-gas octet more cheaply.
And a handy anchor: in the old A-convention, for the s and p block, the group number simply equals the number of valence electrons. So group tells you valence at a glance.
Watch the oxygen scale climb across period three. With respect to oxygen, the valence runs: sodium one, magnesium two, aluminium three, silicon four, phosphorus five, sulphur six, chlorine seven.
The oxides match that climb exactly: sodium oxide, magnesium oxide, aluminium oxide, silicon dioxide, phosphorus pentoxide, sulphur trioxide, and dichlorine heptoxide.
<curious>But the hydrogen scale tells a different story.</curious> With respect to hydrogen, valence rises to a peak and then falls back: one, two, three, four, then three, two, one.
The hydrides show it: sodium hydride, magnesium hydride, aluminium hydride, silane, then phosphine, hydrogen sulphide, and hydrogen chloride.

So hold both patterns. On the oxygen scale valence climbs steadily from one to seven; on the hydrogen scale it rises from one to four and then falls back to one. That difference is a favourite exam point.
चलो valence को precisely pin down करते हैं - formulae predict करने का सबसे useful number।
Representative elements के लिए, valence या तो valence electrons की संख्या है, या eight minus वो संख्या - जो भी route noble-gas octet तक सस्ते में पहुँचे।
और एक handy anchor: पुराने A-convention में, s और p block के लिए, group number बस valence electrons की संख्या के बराबर है। तो group एक नज़र में valence बता देता है।
Oxygen scale को period three के across चढ़ते देखो। Oxygen के respect में, valence चलती है: sodium one, magnesium two, aluminium three, silicon four, phosphorus five, sulphur six, chlorine seven।
Oxides उस climb से बिल्कुल match करते हैं: sodium oxide, magnesium oxide, aluminium oxide, silicon dioxide, phosphorus pentoxide, sulphur trioxide, और dichlorine heptoxide।
<curious>पर hydrogen scale एक अलग कहानी कहता है।</curious> Hydrogen के respect में, valence एक peak तक बढ़ती है फिर वापस गिरती है: one, two, three, four, फिर three, two, one।
Hydrides इसे दिखाते हैं: sodium hydride, magnesium hydride, aluminium hydride, silane, फिर phosphine, hydrogen sulphide, और hydrogen chloride।
तो दोनों patterns पकड़ो। Oxygen scale पर valence steadily one से seven तक चढ़ती है; hydrogen scale पर one से four तक बढ़ती है फिर वापस one पर गिरती है। ये फर्क एक favourite exam point है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Oxidation state: a signed charge by electronegativity

board_events.text: Oxidation state: a signed charge by electronegativity
The charge an atom appears to have when each shared pair is assigned to the more electronegative atom.
In $Na_2O$, oxygen is more electronegative, so O is -2 and Na is +1. In $OF_2$, fluorine wins, so F is -1 and O is +2.
Procedure: give each shared pair to the more electronegative atom; free elements are 0; the states sum to the overall charge.
Group oxidation states climb with configuration: $ns^{1}$ gives +1, up to $ns^{2}np^{5}$ giving -1, +1, +3, +5, +7.
Maximum (group) oxidation state of a $p$-block element equals its total valence electrons.
Lower states differ in steps of two - the inert-pair effect stabilises the lower state down a group ($Tl^{+}, Pb^{2+}$).
Valence is unsigned; oxidation state carries a sign

segments.text: Closely related to valence, but not identical, is the oxidation state - and the difference matters in exams.
The oxidation state is the charge an atom appears to have when every shared electron pair is handed to the more electronegative atom in the bond.

<whisper>Watch how the same oxygen flips sign depending on its partner.</whisper> In sodium oxide, oxygen is more electronegative, so oxygen is minus two and sodium is plus one. But in oxygen difluoride, fluorine is more electronegative, so fluorine is minus one and oxygen is plus two.
The procedure is clean. In each bond, assign the shared pair to the more electronegative atom; a free element is zero; and the oxidation states must sum to the overall charge on the species.

The group oxidation states climb with the valence configuration. n s one gives plus one; n s two gives plus two; and by n s two n p five you have the whole halogen family of minus one, plus one, plus three, plus five, and plus seven.
The key ceiling: the maximum, or group, oxidation state of a p-block element equals its total number of valence electrons - all the s and p electrons together.
And the lower states step down in twos. This is the inert-pair effect - moving down a group, the lower oxidation state becomes more stable, which is why you meet thallium plus one and lead plus two.
So keep valence and oxidation state distinct: valence is an unsigned combining number, while the oxidation state is a signed charge decided by electronegativity.
Valence से closely related, पर identical नहीं, है oxidation state - और ये फर्क exams में matter करता है।
Oxidation state वो charge है जो एक atom के पास दिखता है जब हर shared electron pair bond में ज़्यादा electronegative atom को दे दी जाए।

<whisper>देखो कैसे वही oxygen अपने partner के हिसाब से sign बदलता है।</whisper> Sodium oxide में, oxygen ज़्यादा electronegative है, तो oxygen minus two और sodium plus one। पर oxygen difluoride में, fluorine ज़्यादा electronegative है, तो fluorine minus one और oxygen plus two।
Procedure साफ है। हर bond में, shared pair ज़्यादा electronegative atom को assign करो; free element zero होता है; और oxidation states का जोड़ species के overall charge के बराबर होना चाहिए।

Group oxidation states valence configuration के साथ चढ़ती हैं। n s one देता है plus one; n s two देता है plus two; और n s two n p five तक पहुँचते-पहुँचते पूरा halogen family मिलता है minus one, plus one, plus three, plus five, और plus seven।
Key ceiling: एक p-block element का maximum, या group, oxidation state उसके total valence electrons के बराबर है - सारे s और p electrons मिलाकर।

और lower states दो-दो के steps में उतरते हैं। ये inert-pair effect है - group में नीचे जाते हुए, lower oxidation state ज़्यादा stable हो जाता है, इसीलिए आप thallium plus one और lead plus two से मिलते हो।
तो valence और oxidation state को अलग रखो: valence एक unsigned combining number है, जबकि oxidation state electronegativity से तय एक signed charge है।
