Reducing power sits on the left (electron-givers); oxidising power on the right (electron-grabbers).
One strip captures the whole period's chemistry

segments.text: Let's make the metallic-to-non-metallic shift concrete along period three, from sodium to argon.
The master trend: metallic character and electropositivity fall steadily as you move left to right across a period, while non-metallic character rises.
Down a group the opposite happens - metallic character increases as atoms get bigger and hold their electrons more loosely.
And the oxide character follows this like a shadow: basic oxides on the left, amphoteric in the middle, and acidic oxides on the right.

<curious>Look at the strip for period three.</curious> The left end - sodium, magnesium - is metallic, basic, and reducing. The middle - aluminium, silicon - is the metalloid, amphoteric zone. The right end - phosphorus, sulphur, chlorine - is non-metallic, acidic, and oxidising.

Read the oxide progression printed along it: sodium oxide, magnesium oxide, then aluminium oxide and silicon dioxide in the middle, then phosphorus pentoxide, sulphur trioxide, and dichlorine heptoxide on the acidic right.
And the roles line up. Reducing power lives on the left, with the electron-givers; oxidising power lives on the right, with the electron-grabbers.
That single strip captures the entire chemical personality of a period - which is why examiners can ask so much from just this one figure.
चलो metallic-to-non-metallic shift को period three के साथ concrete बनाते हैं, sodium से argon तक।
Master trend: metallic character और electropositivity steadily गिरते हैं जैसे-जैसे आप period के across left to right जाते हो, जबकि non-metallic character बढ़ता है।
Group में नीचे उल्टा होता है - metallic character बढ़ता है जैसे-जैसे atoms बड़े होते हैं और अपने electrons ज़्यादा loosely पकड़ते हैं।
और oxide character इसे परछाईं की तरह follow करता है: बाईं ओर basic oxides, बीच में amphoteric, और दाईं ओर acidic oxides।

<curious>Period three की strip देखो।</curious> बायाँ सिरा - sodium, magnesium - metallic, basic, और reducing है। बीच - aluminium, silicon - metalloid, amphoteric zone है। दायाँ सिरा - phosphorus, sulphur, chlorine - non-metallic, acidic, और oxidising है।
इसके साथ छपी oxide progression पढ़ो: sodium oxide, magnesium oxide, फिर बीच में aluminium oxide और silicon dioxide, फिर acidic दाईं ओर phosphorus pentoxide, sulphur trioxide, और dichlorine heptoxide।
और roles line up हो जाते हैं। Reducing power बाईं ओर रहती है, electron-givers के साथ; oxidising power दाईं ओर, electron-grabbers के साथ।
वो एक strip पूरे period की chemical personality को समेट लेती है - इसीलिए examiners सिर्फ इस एक figure से इतना कुछ पूछ सकते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: The diagonal relationship

board_events.text: The diagonal relationship
A second-period element resembles the element one step down AND one step to the right.
Classic pairs: Li resembles Mg, Be resembles Al, B resembles Si.
Why: going down a group, size increases; going across to the right, size decreases.
For the first short-period elements these two shifts nearly cancel, leaving similar size and charge-to-radius ratio.
Charge density largely dictates chemistry, so Li behaves more like Mg than like Na.
For example, both Li and Mg form normal oxides (not peroxides like sodium); both Be and Al form amphoteric, covalent-leaning compounds.
Draw the little down-one, right-one shape

segments.text: Here is one of the most elegant patterns in the chapter - the diagonal relationship.
A second-period element resembles not the element directly below it, but the element one step down and one step to the right.
<excited>The classic pairs are worth memorising: lithium resembles magnesium, beryllium resembles aluminium, and boron resembles silicon.</excited>
Why should a diagonal neighbour match? Start from size. Going down a group, atomic and ionic size increases. Going across to the right, size decreases.

For the first, short-period elements, those two shifts very nearly cancel out between an element and its lower-right neighbour - leaving them with comparable size and, crucially, a comparable charge-to-radius ratio.
And since charge density - the polarising power - largely dictates chemistry, lithium ends up behaving more like magnesium than like its own group-mate sodium.

The evidence is concrete. Both lithium and magnesium form normal oxides, not the peroxides that sodium forms. And both beryllium and aluminium form amphoteric, covalent-leaning compounds - very unlike the rest of their groups.
So for any diagonal question, just draw the little shape - down one, right one - and read off the partner. That is all the pattern is.
ये chapter के सबसे elegant patterns में से एक है - diagonal relationship।
एक second-period element उस element जैसा नहीं होता जो सीधे उसके नीचे है, बल्कि उस element जैसा जो एक step नीचे और एक step दाईं ओर है।
<excited>Classic pairs याद रखने लायक हैं: lithium magnesium जैसा, beryllium aluminium जैसा, और boron silicon जैसा।</excited>
एक diagonal neighbour match क्यों करे? Size से शुरू करो। Group में नीचे जाते हुए, atomic और ionic size बढ़ता है। दाईं ओर across जाते हुए, size घटता है।

पहले, short-period elements के लिए, वो दोनों shifts एक element और उसके lower-right neighbour के बीच लगभग cancel हो जाते हैं - जिससे उनका size comparable रह जाता है और, अहम बात, charge-to-radius ratio भी comparable।
और चूँकि charge density - polarising power - काफी हद तक chemistry तय करती है, lithium अपने group-mate sodium से ज़्यादा magnesium जैसा behave करता है।

Evidence concrete है। Lithium और magnesium दोनों normal oxides बनाते हैं, वो peroxides नहीं जो sodium बनाता है। और beryllium और aluminium दोनों amphoteric, covalent-leaning compounds बनाते हैं - अपने बाकी groups से बहुत अलग।
तो किसी भी diagonal question के लिए, बस वो छोटा shape बनाओ - एक नीचे, एक दाईं ओर - और partner पढ़ लो। बस इतना ही है ये pattern।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Why second-period elements break the rules

board_events.text: Why second-period elements break the rules
Lever 1 - smallness and high charge density: the first element of each group polarises electrons strongly, so its compounds lean covalent.
Lever 2 - no valence d-orbitals: period-2 elements have only 2s and 2p available.
With no low-lying 2d subshell to promote into, they cannot expand their octet.
Nitrogen tops out at a covalency of 4 and never forms $NCl_5$ - phosphorus, with empty 3d orbitals, does form $PCl_5$.
Fluorine, lacking d-orbitals and being most electronegative, shows only the -1 state.
Chlorine and below can reach +7 by using their d-orbitals.
Flag: whenever N, O, or F is pushed toward high covalency or an expanded octet, the answer is 'impossible, no d-orbitals'.

segments.text: Now the anomaly that J E E Advanced probes hardest - why the second-period elements refuse to follow their own groups. There are two grounded levers.

The first lever is smallness and high charge density. The first element of each group is so small that it holds and polarises electrons far more strongly than its heavier group-mates, so its compounds lean covalent and its behaviour drifts toward its diagonal neighbour.
<whisper>The second lever is the decisive one.</whisper> Period-two elements have only two s and two p orbitals available in their valence shell - nothing else.
There is no low-lying two d subshell for them to promote an electron into. And without that, they simply cannot expand their octet beyond four orbitals worth of bonds.

So nitrogen tops out at a covalency of four and can never form N C l five. Phosphorus, sitting just below with empty three d orbitals available, happily forms P C l five - the contrast is entirely about orbital availability.
Fluorine takes it to the extreme. Lacking d-orbitals and being the most electronegative element of all, fluorine shows only the minus one state - it is never positive.
Chlorine and the elements below it, by contrast, can reach all the way to plus seven by pressing their d-orbitals into service.
So carry one reflex flag: whenever a question pushes nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine toward a high covalency or an expanded octet, the answer is - impossible, there are no d-orbitals.
अब वो anomaly जिसे J E E Advanced सबसे ज़्यादा probe करता है - second-period elements अपने ही groups को follow करने से क्यों मना करते हैं। इसके दो grounded levers हैं।

पहला lever है smallness और high charge density। हर group का पहला element इतना छोटा है कि वो अपने भारी group-mates से कहीं ज़्यादा strongly electrons पकड़ता और polarise करता है, तो उसके compounds covalent-leaning होते हैं और उसका behaviour अपने diagonal neighbour की तरफ drift करता है।
<whisper>दूसरा lever decisive है।</whisper> Period-two elements के valence shell में सिर्फ two s और two p orbitals available हैं - और कुछ नहीं।
उनके पास promote करने के लिए कोई low-lying two d subshell नहीं है। और उसके बिना, वो अपना octet चार orbitals के bonds से आगे expand ही नहीं कर सकते।

तो nitrogen covalency four पर रुक जाता है और N C l five कभी नहीं बना सकता। Phosphorus, ठीक नीचे बैठा empty three d orbitals के साथ, खुशी-खुशी P C l five बनाता है - ये फर्क पूरी तरह orbital availability का है।
Fluorine इसे extreme पर ले जाता है। d-orbitals न होने और सबसे electronegative element होने के कारण, fluorine सिर्फ minus one state दिखाता है - वो कभी positive नहीं होता।
इसके उलट chlorine और उसके नीचे के elements, अपने d-orbitals को काम में लगाकर plus seven तक पहुँच सकते हैं।
तो एक reflex flag साथ रखो: जब भी कोई question nitrogen, oxygen, या fluorine को high covalency या expanded octet की तरफ धकेले, जवाब है - impossible, कोई d-orbitals नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Worked example: formula from group positions

board_events.text: Worked Example: formula from group positions
Element X is in group 2; element Y is in group 15. Predict the formula and the oxidation states.
Group 2: X reaches the octet by losing 2 electrons - valence 2, forms $X^{2+}$.
Group 15: Y reaches the octet by gaining 3 electrons - valence 3, forms $Y^{3-}$.
Cross-balance the charges: 2 times 3 equals 3 times 2 equals 6, giving the formula $X_3Y_2$.
(b) Oxidation state of X is +2; oxidation state of Y is -3.
The classic slip is writing XY - always cross the valences to balance charge.
Cross the valences, never guess one-to-one

segments.text: Let's apply the valence rules to a classic C B S E board question about combining two elements.
Element X belongs to group two, and element Y to group fifteen. We need the formula of the compound they form, and the oxidation state of each.
Start with X. Being in group two, it reaches its octet most cheaply by losing two electrons, so it has valence two and forms the X two plus ion.
Now Y. In group fifteen, it reaches its octet by gaining three electrons, so it has valence three and forms the Y three minus ion.
<curious>Now cross-balance the charges.</curious> Two times three equals six, and three times two equals six - so we need three X for every two Y. The formula is X three Y two.
For part b, the oxidation states read straight off the ions: X is plus two, and Y is minus three.
The classic slip here is to write X Y, pairing them one-to-one. Always cross the valences to balance the total charge - that is what gives X three Y two.
So the habit is simple: never assume a one-to-one formula, and always cross the combining capacities. It answers a whole family of board questions.
चलो valence rules को दो elements combine करने वाले एक classic C B S E board question पर लगाते हैं।
Element X group two में है, और element Y group fifteen में। हमें उनके बनाए compound का formula चाहिए, और हर एक का oxidation state।
X से शुरू करो। Group two में होने से, वो अपना octet सबसे सस्ते में दो electrons खोकर पाता है, तो उसकी valence two है और वो X two plus ion बनाता है।
अब Y। Group fifteen में, वो अपना octet तीन electrons पाकर पाता है, तो उसकी valence three है और वो Y three minus ion बनाता है।
<curious>अब charges को cross-balance करो।</curious> Two times three बराबर six, और three times two बराबर six - तो हर two Y के लिए तीन X चाहिए। Formula है X three Y two।
Part b के लिए, oxidation states सीधे ions से पढ़ लो: X plus two, और Y minus three।
यहाँ classic slip है X Y लिखना, उन्हें one-to-one pair करके। हमेशा total charge balance करने के लिए valences cross करो - वही X three Y two देता है।
तो आदत simple है: कभी one-to-one formula मत मानो, और हमेशा combining capacities cross करो। ये board questions के पूरे परिवार को answer कर देता है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Worked example: spot the diagonal pair

board_events.text: Worked Example: spot the diagonal pair
Which pair shows a diagonal relationship: (1) Na-Mg, (2) Be-Al, (3) Li-Na, (4) B-C?
Recall the rule: diagonal means the first element of a group resembling its lower-right neighbour.
Na-Mg: same period - not diagonal.
Be-Al: beryllium (group 2, period 2) matches aluminium (group 13, period 3) - one down, one right.
Li-Na: same group. B-C: same period. Neither is the diagonal pattern.
Answer: (2) Be-Al.
The traps are all same-row or same-column pairs

segments.text: This is a N E E T speed trap built entirely around recognising the diagonal pattern.
The question asks which pair shows a diagonal relationship: sodium and magnesium, beryllium and aluminium, lithium and sodium, or boron and carbon?
Don't analyse all four in depth. Just recall the rule: a diagonal relationship is the first element of a group resembling its lower-right neighbour - one step down, one step across.
Sodium and magnesium sit in the same period, side by side - that is not diagonal.
<excited>Beryllium and aluminium is the winner.</excited> Beryllium is group two, period two; aluminium is group thirteen, period three - exactly one down and one to the right.
The rest fall away fast. Lithium and sodium are in the same group. Boron and carbon are in the same period. Neither matches the diagonal shape.
So the answer is option two, beryllium and aluminium.
Notice the trap design: every wrong option is a same-row or same-column pair that looks related but is not the diagonal pattern. Recognise the shape and the distractors collapse.
ये एक N E E T speed trap है जो पूरी तरह diagonal pattern पहचानने के इर्द-गिर्द बना है।
सवाल पूछता है कौन-सा pair diagonal relationship दिखाता है: sodium और magnesium, beryllium और aluminium, lithium और sodium, या boron और carbon?
चारों को गहराई से analyse मत करो। बस rule याद करो: diagonal relationship एक group का पहला element है जो अपने lower-right neighbour जैसा होता है - एक step नीचे, एक step across।
Sodium और magnesium एक ही period में हैं, अगल-बगल - वो diagonal नहीं है।
<excited>Beryllium और aluminium winner है।</excited> Beryllium group two, period two है; aluminium group thirteen, period three - बिल्कुल एक नीचे और एक दाईं ओर।
बाकी तेज़ी से गिर जाते हैं। Lithium और sodium एक ही group में हैं। Boron और carbon एक ही period में। कोई भी diagonal shape से match नहीं करता।
तो जवाब है option two, beryllium और aluminium।
Trap design ध्यान दो: हर गलत option एक same-row या same-column pair है जो related दिखता है पर diagonal pattern नहीं है। Shape पहचानो और distractors ढह जाते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Worked example: from configuration to oxide character

board_events.text: Worked Example: from configuration to oxide character
Element Z has valence-shell configuration $ns^{2}np^{4}$. Find its group, oxidation-state range, and highest oxide.
(a) $ns^{2}np^{4}$ means 6 valence electrons, so Z is in Group 16.
(b) Minimum state: gain 2 electrons to complete the octet, giving -2.
Maximum (group) state equals total valence electrons: +6.
(c) In the +6 state the highest oxide is $ZO_3$.
Group 16 lies on the non-metallic right, so its highest oxide is acidic - analogous to $SO_3$, which gives sulphuric acid with water.
Configuration to group to oxidation range to oxide

segments.text: Now a J E E Main question that stitches three skills into one chain - configuration, oxidation range, and oxide character.
Element Z has the valence-shell configuration n s two n p four. We need its group, its minimum and maximum oxidation states, and the formula and nature of its highest oxide.
Part a. The configuration n s two n p four adds up to six valence electrons, which places Z squarely in group sixteen.
Part b, the minimum state. With six valence electrons, the cheapest route to an octet is to gain two more, giving a minimum oxidation state of minus two.
<curious>And the maximum follows the group rule.</curious> The maximum, or group, oxidation state equals the total valence electrons - here that is plus six.
Part c, the highest oxide. In its plus six state, Z bonds with three oxygens, so the highest oxide has the formula Z O three.
And its nature? Group sixteen sits on the non-metallic right of the table, so its highest oxide is acidic - directly analogous to sulphur trioxide, which reacts with water to give sulphuric acid.
So the chain runs cleanly: configuration to group, group to oxidation-state range, and metallic position to oxide character. That single chain answers the whole question.
अब एक J E E Main question जो तीन skills को एक chain में जोड़ता है - configuration, oxidation range, और oxide character।
Element Z की valence-shell configuration n s two n p four है। हमें उसका group, उसके minimum और maximum oxidation states, और उसके highest oxide का formula और nature चाहिए।
Part a। Configuration n s two n p four जुड़कर छह valence electrons बनता है, जो Z को सीधे group sixteen में रखता है।
Part b, minimum state। छह valence electrons के साथ, octet तक सबसे सस्ता route है दो और gain करना, जिससे minimum oxidation state minus two।
<curious>और maximum group rule follow करता है।</curious> Maximum, या group, oxidation state total valence electrons के बराबर है - यहाँ वो plus six है।
Part c, highest oxide। अपने plus six state में, Z तीन oxygens से bond करता है, तो highest oxide का formula Z O three है।
और उसका nature? Group sixteen table के non-metallic दाईं ओर बैठता है, तो उसका highest oxide acidic है - सीधे sulphur trioxide जैसा, जो पानी से react करके sulphuric acid देता है।
तो chain साफ चलती है: configuration से group, group से oxidation-state range, और metallic position से oxide character। वो एक chain पूरे question को answer कर देती है।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Worked example: why PCl5 exists but NCl5 does not

board_events.text: Worked Example: why PCl5 exists but NCl5 does not
(a) To form five bonds, an atom must unpair its $ns^{2}$ and promote one electron into an empty valence orbital - giving five singly-occupied orbitals.
Phosphorus ($[Ne]3s^{2}3p^{3}$) has empty low-lying 3d orbitals to receive the promoted electron, so it forms $PCl_5$.
Nitrogen ($[He]2s^{2}2p^{3}$) has no 2d orbitals; the next available subshell, 3s, is far too high in energy.
With no way past four orbitals (2s + 2p), nitrogen cannot make five bonds - $NCl_5$ does not exist.
(b) Nitrogen's maximum covalency is 4 (one 2s plus three 2p orbitals); it reaches 4 in $NH_4^{+}$ but never higher.
(c) Oxygen is also period 2 with no 2d orbitals, so it cannot host six bonds - no $OF_6$, no +6 state; its typical maximum is +2, as in $OF_2$.
The barrier is orbital availability, not thermodynamics

segments.text: We finish with the J E E Advanced question that gets to the very root of the second-period anomaly - why phosphorus forms P C l five but nitrogen, directly above it, does not form N C l five.

Part a, the orbital argument. To form five bonds, an atom must unpair its n s two electrons and promote one of them into an empty valence orbital, so that it has five singly-occupied orbitals ready to bond.

Phosphorus, with configuration neon core three s two three p three, has empty, low-lying three d orbitals sitting right there to receive that promoted electron. So it reaches five unpaired electrons and forms P C l five with ease.

<whisper>Nitrogen has no such escape.</whisper> Its configuration is helium core two s two two p three, and there are no two d orbitals at all - the next available subshell, three s, is far too high in energy to use.
With no way to expand beyond the four orbitals of two s and two p, nitrogen simply cannot make five bonds. N C l five does not exist - and the barrier is orbital availability, not mere instability.

Part b. Nitrogen's maximum covalency is therefore four - one two s plus three two p orbitals. It can reach four, for instance in the ammonium ion by donating its lone pair, but it can never go higher.

Part c generalises to oxygen. Oxygen is also a second-period element with only two s and two p orbitals and no two d. So it cannot host six bonds - there is no oxygen hexafluoride and no plus six state the way sulphur manages in sulphur hexafluoride. Oxygen's typical maximum is plus two, as in oxygen difluoride.
The deep lesson: for nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine, the ceiling on bonding is set by orbital availability, not by thermodynamics. No d-orbitals means no expanded octet - full stop.
हम उस J E E Advanced question से खत्म करते हैं जो second-period anomaly की जड़ तक पहुँचता है - phosphorus P C l five क्यों बनाता है पर nitrogen, ठीक उसके ऊपर, N C l five क्यों नहीं बनाता।

Part a, orbital argument। पाँच bonds बनाने के लिए, एक atom को अपने n s two electrons unpair करने होते हैं और उनमें से एक को empty valence orbital में promote करना होता है, ताकि उसके पास bond के लिए तैयार पाँच singly-occupied orbitals हों।

Phosphorus, configuration neon core three s two three p three के साथ, empty, low-lying three d orbitals रखता है जो ठीक वहीं मौजूद हैं उस promoted electron को लेने के लिए। तो वो पाँच unpaired electrons तक पहुँचता है और आसानी से P C l five बनाता है।

<whisper>Nitrogen के पास ऐसा कोई escape नहीं।</whisper> उसकी configuration helium core two s two two p three है, और two d orbitals हैं ही नहीं - अगला available subshell, three s, इस्तेमाल करने के लिए energy में बहुत ऊँचा है।

Two s और two p के चार orbitals से आगे expand करने का कोई रास्ता न होने से, nitrogen पाँच bonds बना ही नहीं सकता। N C l five exist नहीं करता - और barrier orbital availability है, महज़ instability नहीं।
Part b। इसलिए nitrogen की maximum covalency चार है - एक two s plus तीन two p orbitals। वो चार तक पहुँच सकता है, जैसे ammonium ion में अपनी lone pair donate करके, पर इससे ऊपर कभी नहीं।

Part c oxygen पर generalise होता है। Oxygen भी एक second-period element है जिसके पास सिर्फ two s और two p orbitals हैं, कोई two d नहीं। तो वो छह bonds host नहीं कर सकता - कोई oxygen hexafluoride नहीं और कोई plus six state नहीं जैसा sulphur, sulphur hexafluoride में करता है। Oxygen का typical maximum plus two है, जैसे oxygen difluoride में।
गहरा lesson: nitrogen, oxygen, और fluorine के लिए, bonding की ceiling orbital availability से तय होती है, thermodynamics से नहीं। कोई d-orbitals नहीं यानी कोई expanded octet नहीं - बस।

sections.subtopic: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties & Anomalous Behaviour
sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Common pitfalls and pro-tips
Pitfall 1: formula crossover slips. Combining a group-2 with a group-15 element gives $X_3Y_2$, not XY - always cross the valences.
Pitfall 2: confusing diagonal pairs with group or period neighbours. Diagonal means first element and its lower-right neighbour: Li-Mg, Be-Al, B-Si.
Pitfall 3: mis-counting the maximum oxidation state. The group state uses all valence s and p electrons, not 8 minus N.
Pitfall 4: granting octet expansion to period-2 atoms. N, O, F have no d-orbitals - pentavalent N or hexavalent O simply do not exist.
Reflex 1: left gives, right grabs - metallic, basic, reducing on the left; non-metallic, acidic, oxidising on the right; reactivity peaks at both ends.
Reflex 2: the 'period-2 has no d' flag - push N, O, or F toward an expanded octet and the answer is 'impossible'.
For diagonal questions, draw the little down-one, right-one shape and read off the partner.

segments.text: Let's close the subtopic with the traps that cost marks and the reflexes that save time.

<whisper>Pitfall one is the formula crossover slip.</whisper> When you combine a group-two element with a group-fifteen one, the formula is X three Y two, not X Y. Always cross the valences to balance the charge.

Pitfall two: confusing diagonal pairs with ordinary group or period neighbours. Diagonal means the first element of a group and its lower-right neighbour - lithium-magnesium, beryllium-aluminium, boron-silicon. Same-row and same-column pairs are not it.
Pitfall three: mis-counting the maximum oxidation state. The group state uses all the valence s and p electrons - it is not eight minus N, which gives the anionic valence instead.
Pitfall four: granting octet expansion to a period-two atom. Nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine have no d-orbitals, so a pentavalent nitrogen or a hexavalent oxygen simply does not exist.

Now the pro-tips - two reflexes that carry most questions. Reflex one: left gives, right grabs. Metallic, basic, and reducing behaviour on the left; non-metallic, acidic, and oxidising on the right; and reactivity peaking at both ends of the period.
Reflex two: the period-two has no d flag. The moment a question pushes nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine toward an expanded octet or high covalency, the answer is - impossible.
And for any diagonal question, just draw the little down-one, right-one shape and read the partner straight off. Between these reflexes, most of this subtopic answers itself.
चलो subtopic को उन traps से बंद करते हैं जो marks खाते हैं और उन reflexes से जो time बचाते हैं।

<whisper>Pitfall one है formula crossover slip।</whisper> जब आप एक group-two element को group-fifteen वाले से combine करते हो, formula X three Y two है, X Y नहीं। हमेशा charge balance करने के लिए valences cross करो।

Pitfall two: diagonal pairs को आम group या period neighbours से confuse करना। Diagonal मतलब एक group का पहला element और उसका lower-right neighbour - lithium-magnesium, beryllium-aluminium, boron-silicon। Same-row और same-column pairs वो नहीं हैं।
Pitfall three: maximum oxidation state गलत गिनना। Group state सारे valence s और p electrons इस्तेमाल करता है - ये eight minus N नहीं है, जो उसकी जगह anionic valence देता है।
Pitfall four: एक period-two atom को octet expansion देना। Nitrogen, oxygen, और fluorine के पास कोई d-orbitals नहीं, तो pentavalent nitrogen या hexavalent oxygen exist ही नहीं करता।

अब pro-tips - दो reflexes जो ज़्यादातर questions उठा लेते हैं। Reflex one: left gives, right grabs। बाईं ओर metallic, basic, और reducing behaviour; दाईं ओर non-metallic, acidic, और oxidising; और reactivity period के दोनों सिरों पर peak करती है।
Reflex two: period-two has no d वाला flag। जिस पल कोई question nitrogen, oxygen, या fluorine को expanded octet या high covalency की तरफ धकेले, जवाब है - impossible।
और किसी भी diagonal question के लिए, बस वो छोटा down-one, right-one shape बनाओ और partner सीधे पढ़ लो। इन reflexes के बीच, ये subtopic ज़्यादातर खुद को answer कर देता है।

sections.title: Position is a picture of electronic configuration

board_events.text: Position is a picture of electronic configuration
Everything so far - history, size trends, reactivity - rests on one quiet fact.
An element's position in the table is simply a picture of its electronic configuration.
Think of the table as a giant multi-storey housing colony. Each floor is a period; the floor number is the outermost shell n.
Electrons move in one at a time, always taking the lowest-energy room available - the Aufbau principle.
The type of room the newest electron checks into - s, p, d, or f - decides the block.
Two ideas: Period number = highest principal quantum number n. Block = subshell of the last (differentiating) electron.
Derive an element's address; never memorise it

segments.text: We reach the foundation that quietly holds up the whole chapter. Everything from the last three subtopics - the table's history, the size trends, the reactivity patterns - all of it rests on one simple fact.
That fact is this: an element's position in the periodic table is nothing more than a picture of its electronic configuration.

<curious>The table is not an arbitrary filing cabinet - it is a map of how electrons fill orbitals.</curious> Once you truly see that, you never have to memorise where an element sits; you can derive it.
Here is the picture. Think of the periodic table as a giant multi-storey housing colony. Each floor is a period, and the floor number tells you the outermost shell, n, that the residents live on.
As you build the colony from the ground up, electrons move in one at a time, always taking the lowest-energy room available. That is just the Aufbau principle from your atomic-structure chapter.
And the type of room the newest electron checks into - an s, p, d, or f room - decides which block, which wing of the building, the element belongs to.

So hold two organising ideas. The period number equals the highest principal quantum number, n, in the configuration. And the block is fixed by the subshell that receives the last, differentiating electron.
With just those two, you stop memorising the table and start deriving each element's address - which is exactly what the exam rewards.
हम उस foundation तक पहुँचते हैं जो चुपचाप पूरे chapter को थामे रखती है। पिछले तीन subtopics का सब कुछ - table का इतिहास, size trends, reactivity patterns - ये सब एक simple fact पर टिका है।
वो fact ये है: periodic table में element की position उसकी electronic configuration की एक तस्वीर से ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं।

<curious>Table कोई arbitrary filing cabinet नहीं - ये एक map है कि electrons orbitals कैसे भरते हैं।</curious> एक बार आप ये सच में देख लो, तो कभी याद नहीं रखना पड़ता कि element कहाँ बैठता है; आप उसे derive कर सकते हो।
ये रही तस्वीर। Periodic table को एक बड़ी multi-storey housing colony समझो। हर floor एक period है, और floor number बताता है वो outermost shell, n, जिस पर residents रहते हैं।
जैसे-जैसे आप colony को नीचे से ऊपर बनाते हो, electrons एक-एक करके आते हैं, हमेशा सबसे कम-energy वाला available room लेते हुए। ये बस आपके atomic-structure chapter का Aufbau principle है।
और सबसे नया electron जिस तरह के room में check-in करता है - s, p, d, या f room - वो तय करता है कि element किस block में, building के किस wing में है।
तो दो organising ideas पकड़ो। Period number configuration में highest principal quantum number, n, के बराबर है। और block उस subshell से fix होता है जो आखिरी, differentiating electron लेता है।
बस इन दो के साथ, आप table रटना बंद कर देते हो और हर element का address derive करना शुरू कर देते हो - जो बिल्कुल वही है जो exam reward करता है।

board_events.text: The shape 2, then 10, then 6 (with 14 below) is just the seating capacity of the s, d, p (and f) subshells.
The table's outline is subshell capacity made visible

segments.text: Let's walk the corridor of that housing colony and meet the four blocks - and see why the table has its distinctive shape.
On each floor there is a long corridor of doors. The first two doors on the left are the s-rooms. Elements whose newest electron checks in here form the s-block.
At the far right of the corridor are six more doors - the p-rooms - giving the p-block.

Then, starting from the fourth floor, a set of ten extra rooms appears tucked into the middle of the corridor. These are the d-rooms, the d-block or transition metals - and they are numbered as belonging to the floor below, written n minus one d.

And from the sixth floor onward, fourteen more rooms are hidden in a basement annexe - the f-rooms, the f-block or inner-transition metals, pulled out and printed separately below the main chart so it stays a sensible width.

<excited>Look at the schematic - four coloured regions, each with its valence configuration.</excited> The s-block on the left, the p-block on the right, the d-block filling the centre, and the f-block strip drawn below, with the metalloid staircase zig-zagging through the p-block.
So the whole outline of the table - two columns, then ten, then six, with fourteen printed below - is nothing but the seating capacity of the s, d, and p subshells, plus the f annexe.
That is worth pausing on: the table's shape is not decorative, it is subshell capacity made visible. Two, ten, six, fourteen - that is the entire silhouette.
चलो उस housing colony के corridor में चलते हैं और चारों blocks से मिलते हैं - और देखते हैं कि table का ये खास shape क्यों है।
हर floor पर doors का एक लंबा corridor है। बाईं ओर के पहले दो doors s-rooms हैं। जिन elements का सबसे नया electron यहाँ check-in करता है, वो s-block बनाते हैं।
Corridor के सबसे दाईं ओर छह और doors हैं - p-rooms - जो p-block देते हैं।

फिर, चौथी floor से शुरू होकर, दस extra rooms का एक set corridor के बीच में tucked हुआ दिखता है। ये d-rooms हैं, d-block या transition metals - और इन्हें नीचे वाली floor का माना जाता है, n minus one d लिखा जाता है।

और छठी floor से आगे, चौदह और rooms एक basement annexe में छुपे हैं - f-rooms, f-block या inner-transition metals, जिन्हें main chart के नीचे अलग निकालकर print किया जाता है ताकि chart की width sensible रहे।

<excited>Schematic देखो - चार coloured regions, हर एक अपनी valence configuration के साथ।</excited> बाईं ओर s-block, दाईं ओर p-block, बीच में d-block, और नीचे बनी f-block strip, और p-block में से zig-zag करती metalloid staircase।
तो table का पूरा outline - दो columns, फिर दस, फिर छह, और नीचे चौदह print - बस s, d, और p subshells की seating capacity है, plus f annexe।
इस पर रुकना फायदेमंद है: table का shape सजावट नहीं, subshell capacity को visible बनाया गया है। Two, ten, six, fourteen - यही पूरा silhouette है।

sections.subtopic: Electronic Configuration & the s, p, d, f Blocks
sections.title: The four blocks and their character

board_events.text: The four blocks and their character
s-block (groups 1-2, $ns^{1-2}$): reactive metals, lowest IE, strong reducing agents, ionic compounds, basic oxides.
p-block (groups 13-18, $ns^{2}np^{1-6}$): the only block spanning metals, metalloids, non-metals and noble gases.
p-block oxides shift basic to amphoteric to acidic across each period; oxidation states differ in steps of two.
d-block (groups 3-12, $(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}$): transition metals - variable oxidation states, coloured ions, paramagnetism, complexes, catalysts.
d-block draws on both $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons - the source of all those hallmark traits.
f-block ($(n-2)f^{1-14}$): inner-transition metals; the differentiating electron sits two shells deep, so a series behaves alike.
Block decides character, character decides chemistry

segments.text: Now let's give each of the four blocks its chemical personality - because the block an element sits in largely predicts how it behaves.

The s-block, groups one and two with valence configuration n s one to two, holds its outer electrons loosely. So these are reactive metals with the lowest ionisation enthalpies in their periods - strong reducing agents, forming ionic compounds and strongly basic oxides and hydroxides.
The p-block, groups thirteen to eighteen with n s two n p one to six, is special: it is the only block that spans metals, metalloids, non-metals, and the noble gases all at once.

That is why it shows the widest variety of chemistry. Its oxides shift from basic through amphoteric to acidic across each period, and its oxidation states differ in steps of two - the group state and group minus two, via the inert-pair effect lower down.

<excited>The d-block, groups three to twelve with n minus one d one to ten and n s zero to two, are the transition metals.</excited> Their hallmark traits: variable oxidation states, coloured ions, paramagnetism, a strong tendency to form complexes, and heavy use as catalysts.
And the reason for all of that is one fact - the d-block draws on both its n minus one d and its n s electrons for bonding. Two sets of electrons in play gives all those rich behaviours.

Finally the f-block, with valence configuration n minus two f one to fourteen, are the inner-transition metals. Their differentiating electron sits two shells deep, so the outer shells barely change across a series - which is why the lanthanoids behave remarkably alike, mostly in the plus three state.
So the logic is clean: the block decides the character, and the character decides the chemistry. Name the block and you already know a great deal.
अब चारों blocks को उनकी chemical personality देते हैं - क्योंकि element जिस block में बैठता है वो काफी हद तक बता देता है कि वो कैसे behave करेगा।

s-block, groups one और two, valence configuration n s one to two के साथ, अपने outer electrons loosely पकड़ता है। तो ये reactive metals हैं अपने periods में सबसे कम ionisation enthalpies के साथ - strong reducing agents, ionic compounds और strongly basic oxides व hydroxides बनाते हुए।
p-block, groups thirteen to eighteen, n s two n p one to six के साथ, खास है: ये इकलौता block है जो एक साथ metals, metalloids, non-metals, और noble gases सब को फैलाता है।

इसीलिए ये सबसे ज़्यादा variety की chemistry दिखाता है। इसके oxides हर period के across basic से amphoteric से acidic में shift होते हैं, और इसके oxidation states दो-दो के steps में फर्क करते हैं - group state और group minus two, नीचे inert-pair effect से।

<excited>d-block, groups three to twelve, n minus one d one to ten और n s zero to two के साथ, transition metals हैं।</excited> इनके hallmark traits: variable oxidation states, coloured ions, paramagnetism, complexes बनाने की strong tendency, और catalysts के रूप में भारी इस्तेमाल।
और इन सबकी वजह एक fact है - d-block bonding के लिए अपने n minus one d और n s दोनों electrons पर निर्भर करता है। दो sets electrons खेल में होने से ये सारे rich behaviours मिलते हैं।

आखिर में f-block, valence configuration n minus two f one to fourteen के साथ, inner-transition metals हैं। इनका differentiating electron दो shells गहरे बैठता है, तो outer shells एक series के across मुश्किल से बदलते हैं - इसीलिए lanthanoids हैरानी की हद तक एक जैसे behave करते हैं, ज़्यादातर plus three state में।
तो logic साफ है: block character तय करता है, और character chemistry तय करती है। Block का नाम बताओ और आप पहले से बहुत कुछ जान जाते हो।

sections.subtopic: Electronic Configuration & the s, p, d, f Blocks
sections.title: Four types of elements

board_events.text: Four types of elements
Representative (main-group): the s- and p-block together, groups 1, 2 and 13-17; last electron enters the outermost shell.
Noble gases: group 18, filled valence shell $ns^{2}np^{6}$ (He is $1s^{2}$); highest IE, chemically inert.
Transition elements: the d-block. Strict definition - a partially filled d-subshell in the atom OR in a stable ion.
By that strict rule, zinc, cadmium, mercury ($d^{10}$) are NOT true transition metals, though they sit in the d-block.
Inner-transition elements: the f-block - lanthanoids (filling 4f) and actinoids (filling 5f).
Metals are about 80 percent of elements; non-metals cluster upper-right; metalloids run the staircase B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te.
The strict d-rule is the favourite exam trap

segments.text: The blocks also sort into four named types of element, and one definition here is a favourite exam trap.
First, the representative or main-group elements - the s-block and p-block together, groups one, two, and thirteen to seventeen. Their last electron enters the outermost shell.

Second, the noble gases of group eighteen, with a completely filled valence shell - n s two n p six, except helium which is one s two. They have the highest ionisation enthalpies in their periods and are essentially inert.

<whisper>Third, the transition elements - the d-block - and here is the strict definition to lock in.</whisper> A transition element has a partially filled d-subshell, either in the neutral atom or in a stable ion.
By that strict rule, zinc, cadmium, and mercury - all d ten - are not true transition metals, even though they sit inside the d-block by position. That distinction is tested almost every year.
Fourth, the inner-transition elements - the f-block. These are the lanthanoids, which fill the four f subshell, and the actinoids, which fill the five f.

And overlaying all of this: metals make up about eighty percent of the elements, sitting left, centre, and lower-right; non-metals cluster at the upper right of the p-block; and the metalloids run along the staircase - boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium.
So keep that strict d-rule sharp: sitting in the d-block is not the same as being a transition metal. That single distinction catches more students than almost anything else here.
Blocks चार named types of element में भी बँटते हैं, और यहाँ एक definition favourite exam trap है।
पहला, representative या main-group elements - s-block और p-block मिलाकर, groups one, two, और thirteen to seventeen। इनका last electron outermost shell में जाता है।

दूसरा, group eighteen के noble gases, पूरी तरह filled valence shell के साथ - n s two n p six, सिवाय helium के जो one s two है। इनकी अपने periods में सबसे ऊँची ionisation enthalpies हैं और ये लगभग inert हैं।

<whisper>तीसरा, transition elements - d-block - और यहाँ lock करने वाली strict definition है।</whisper> एक transition element का d-subshell partially filled होता है, या तो neutral atom में या किसी stable ion में।
उस strict rule से, zinc, cadmium, और mercury - सब d ten - true transition metals नहीं हैं, भले position से d-block के अंदर बैठते हों। वो distinction लगभग हर साल test होता है।
चौथा, inner-transition elements - f-block। ये lanthanoids हैं, जो four f subshell भरते हैं, और actinoids, जो five f भरते हैं।

और इन सब पर overlay: metals करीब अस्सी percent elements हैं, बाईं ओर, बीच में, और lower-right बैठे; non-metals p-block के upper right में cluster करते हैं; और metalloids staircase पर चलते हैं - boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium।
तो उस strict d-rule को तेज़ रखो: d-block में बैठना transition metal होने के बराबर नहीं है। वो एक distinction यहाँ लगभग किसी भी और चीज़ से ज़्यादा students को पकड़ता है।

sections.subtopic: Electronic Configuration & the s, p, d, f Blocks
sections.title: From atomic number to period, block, and group

board_events.text: From atomic number to period, block, and group
Step 1: write the configuration in Aufbau order - 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p and so on.
Step 2: the period is the largest principal quantum number n that appears.
Step 3: the block is the subshell of the last electron added - s, p, $(n-1)d$, or $(n-2)f$.
Step 4, group rules: s-block = number of $ns$ electrons; p-block = 10 + (outer $ns + np$); d-block = $(n-1)d + ns$.
Why: the group number counts the electrons available for bonding.
For s and p that is the outer-shell electrons (shifted by ten for the p-block); for d-block both $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ participate.
Four steps place almost any element

segments.text: Now the workhorse procedure - turning any atomic number into a period, a block, and a group. Four clean steps.
Step one: write the electronic configuration in the Aufbau filling order - one s, two s, two p, three s, three p, four s, three d, four p, and so on.
Step two: read off the period as the largest principal quantum number, n, that appears anywhere in the configuration.
Step three: identify the block from the subshell that received the last electron - s, p, n minus one d, or n minus two f.

<curious>Step four is the group, and it is block-specific.</curious> For the s-block, the group equals the number of n s electrons. For the p-block, it is ten plus the outer n s and n p electrons. For the d-block, it is the n minus one d electrons plus the n s electrons.
Why do these rules work? Because the group number ultimately counts the electrons available for bonding.

For the s and p elements that is just the outer-shell electrons - shifted by ten for the p-block because groups three to twelve sit in between. For the d-block, both the n minus one d and the n s electrons take part in bonding, so you count both.
With these four steps, you can place almost any element on the table from its atomic number alone - which is exactly the J E E Main one-shot question.
अब workhorse procedure - किसी भी atomic number को period, block, और group में बदलना। चार साफ steps।
Step one: electronic configuration को Aufbau filling order में लिखो - one s, two s, two p, three s, three p, four s, three d, four p, और आगे।
Step two: period को उस largest principal quantum number, n, के रूप में पढ़ो जो configuration में कहीं भी दिखे।
Step three: block को उस subshell से पहचानो जिसने last electron लिया - s, p, n minus one d, या n minus two f।

<curious>Step four है group, और ये block-specific है।</curious> s-block के लिए, group n s electrons की संख्या के बराबर है। p-block के लिए, ये ten plus outer n s और n p electrons है। d-block के लिए, ये n minus one d electrons plus n s electrons है।
ये rules काम क्यों करते हैं? क्योंकि group number आखिरकार bonding के लिए available electrons गिनता है।

s और p elements के लिए वो बस outer-shell electrons हैं - p-block के लिए ten से shifted क्योंकि groups three to twelve बीच में बैठते हैं। d-block के लिए, n minus one d और n s दोनों electrons bonding में हिस्सा लेते हैं, तो आप दोनों गिनते हो।
इन चार steps के साथ, आप लगभग किसी भी element को सिर्फ उसके atomic number से table पर place कर सकते हो - जो बिल्कुल वो J E E Main one-shot question है।

sections.subtopic: Electronic Configuration & the s, p, d, f Blocks
sections.title: The predictable exceptions: Cr, Cu, He, H

board_events.text: The predictable exceptions: Cr, Cu, He, H
A few d-block elements defy naive Aufbau because half-filled ($d^{5}$) and fully filled ($d^{10}$) subshells are extra stable.
Chromium: expected $[Ar]3d^{4}4s^{2}$, actual $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ - one 4s electron shifts to reach the stable $d^{5}$.
Copper: expected $[Ar]3d^{9}4s^{2}$, actual $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^{1}$ - to reach the stable $d^{10}$.
The extra stability comes from symmetry, minimum electron repulsion, and exchange energy. The block stays d either way.
Helium: $1s^{2}$ looks s-block, yet it is placed in group 18 - its full valence shell makes it a noble gas. Property wins.
Hydrogen: $1s^{1}$ resembles both alkali metals (one valence electron) and halogens (one short of a shell) - group 1 is a convenience.
These are predictable exceptions, not failures

segments.text: Finally, the exceptions - and the key insight is that they are predictable, not failures of the theory.
A handful of d-block elements deviate from a naive Aufbau filling, because an exactly half-filled d five and a completely filled d ten subshell are especially stable.

Chromium is the classic case. Naive filling predicts argon core, three d four, four s two. But the actual configuration is argon core, three d five, four s one - one four s electron shifts across into three d to reach that stable, half-filled d five.

<excited>Copper does the same thing one step further.</excited> Naive filling predicts three d nine, four s two, but the actual is three d ten, four s one - one four s electron moves over to complete the stable, fully-filled d ten.

Where does the stability come from? Three sources - the symmetry of a half- or fully-filled set, the minimum electron-electron repulsion, and the extra exchange energy. Importantly, the block stays d either way; only the fine configuration shifts.

Two placement oddities round it off. Helium is one s two, which looks like an s-block element, yet it is placed in group eighteen - because its completely filled valence shell makes it behave as a noble gas. Here property wins over bare configuration.

And hydrogen, one s one, refuses to settle. It resembles the alkali metals with its single valence electron, but also the halogens, being one electron short of a stable shell. Its placement in group one is a convenience, not a perfect fit.

So treat all four as predictable exceptions. Reach reflexively for the half-filled or fully-filled explanation at chromium and copper, and remember that helium and hydrogen are placed by property and convenience.
आखिर में, exceptions - और key insight ये है कि ये predictable हैं, theory की failures नहीं।
मुट्ठी भर d-block elements naive Aufbau filling से हटते हैं, क्योंकि exactly half-filled d five और completely filled d ten subshell खास तौर पर stable हैं।

Chromium classic case है। Naive filling predict करता है argon core, three d four, four s two। पर actual configuration है argon core, three d five, four s one - एक four s electron three d में shift हो जाता है उस stable, half-filled d five तक पहुँचने के लिए।

<excited>Copper एक कदम आगे वही करता है।</excited> Naive filling predict करता है three d nine, four s two, पर actual है three d ten, four s one - एक four s electron चला जाता है stable, fully-filled d ten पूरा करने के लिए।

ये stability कहाँ से आती है? तीन sources - half या fully-filled set की symmetry, minimum electron-electron repulsion, और extra exchange energy। अहम बात, block दोनों case में d रहता है; सिर्फ fine configuration shift होती है।

दो placement oddities इसे पूरा करती हैं। Helium one s two है, जो एक s-block element जैसा दिखता है, फिर भी उसे group eighteen में रखा जाता है - क्योंकि उसका completely filled valence shell उसे noble gas की तरह behave कराता है। यहाँ property bare configuration पर जीत जाती है।

और hydrogen, one s one, टिकने से मना कर देता है। ये alkali metals जैसा लगता है अपने अकेले valence electron से, पर halogens जैसा भी, एक electron से stable shell में कम होने से। इसका group one में placement एक convenience है, perfect fit नहीं।
तो चारों को predictable exceptions मानो। Chromium और copper पर reflexively half-filled या fully-filled explanation की तरफ बढ़ो, और याद रखो कि helium और hydrogen property और convenience से रखे गए हैं।

sections.subtopic: Electronic Configuration & the s, p, d, f Blocks
sections.title: Worked example: place the element with Z = 38

board_events.text: Worked Example: place the element with Z = 38
Write the configuration for $Z = 38$ and state its period, group, and block.
(a) Highest n is 5, so it is in period 5.
(b) Last electron entered 5s, so it is s-block; group = number of $ns$ electrons = 2.
(c) A group-2, s-block, period-5 element - an alkaline earth metal.
This element is strontium.
Configuration first, then read off all three

segments.text: Let's run the placement procedure on a classic C B S E question - the element with atomic number thirty eight.
We need to write its electronic configuration and then state its period, its group, and its block.

Building up in Aufbau order gives one s two, two s two, two p six, three s two, three p six, four s two, three d ten, four p six, five s two - which we can write compactly as krypton core, five s two.
<curious>Part a, the period.</curious> The highest principal quantum number appearing is five, so this element is in period five.
Part b, the block and group. The last electron entered the five s subshell, so it is an s-block element; and the group equals the number of n s electrons, which is two.
Part c: putting it together, this is a group-two, s-block, period-five element - an alkaline earth metal.
And that pins it down uniquely: the element with atomic number thirty eight is strontium.
The habit to carry: always write the configuration first, then read the period, block, and group straight off it. Never try to place the element by memory alone.
चलो placement procedure को एक classic C B S E question पर चलाते हैं - atomic number thirty eight वाला element।
हमें इसकी electronic configuration लिखनी है और फिर इसका period, group, और block बताना है।

Aufbau order में build करने पर मिलता है one s two, two s two, two p six, three s two, three p six, four s two, three d ten, four p six, five s two - जिसे हम compactly krypton core, five s two लिख सकते हैं।
<curious>Part a, period।</curious> सबसे ऊँचा principal quantum number जो दिखता है वो five है, तो ये element period five में है।
Part b, block और group। Last electron five s subshell में गया, तो ये s-block element है; और group n s electrons की संख्या के बराबर है, जो two है।
Part c: जोड़कर, ये एक group-two, s-block, period-five element है - एक alkaline earth metal।
और ये इसे uniquely pin कर देता है: atomic number thirty eight वाला element strontium है।
साथ ले जाने वाली आदत: हमेशा पहले configuration लिखो, फिर period, block, और group सीधे उससे पढ़ो। Element को कभी सिर्फ याददाश्त से place करने की कोशिश मत करो।

sections.subtopic: Electronic Configuration & the s, p, d, f Blocks
sections.title: Worked example: which is a representative element?

board_events.text: Worked Example: which is a representative element?
Which has a representative element: $Z = 24$, $Z = 12$, $Z = 26$, or $Z = 29$?
Representative = s- or p-block (groups 1, 2, 13-17). Just locate each; don't write full configurations.
$Z = 12$ (magnesium): $[Ne]3s^{2}$ - s-block, representative.
$Z = 24$ (chromium), $Z = 26$ (iron), $Z = 29$ (copper): all in the 3d series - d-block, transition.
Answer: $Z = 12$, magnesium.
The three traps are all transition metals; students who forget that representative excludes the d-block fall for them.
Representative means s or p only

segments.text: This is a N E E T speed trap that turns on one definition - what counts as a representative element.
The question offers four atomic numbers - twenty four, twelve, twenty six, and twenty nine - and asks which is a representative element.
<curious>Recall the definition: representative means s-block or p-block only, groups one, two, and thirteen to seventeen.</curious> Don't write full configurations; just locate each one.
Atomic number twelve is magnesium - neon core, three s two. Its last electron is in the s subshell, so it is s-block, and therefore representative. That is our answer.
The other three all sit in the three d series. Twenty four is chromium, twenty six is iron, twenty nine is copper - every one of them a d-block transition metal.
So the answer is atomic number twelve, magnesium.
Notice the trap: all three distractors are transition metals. A student who forgets that representative elements exclude the d-block will be tempted straight into a wrong choice.
So carry it crisply: representative means s or p only. The moment you see a three d element, it is out of the running.
ये एक N E E T speed trap है जो एक definition पर टिका है - representative element क्या माना जाता है।
सवाल चार atomic numbers देता है - twenty four, twelve, twenty six, और twenty nine - और पूछता है कौन-सा representative element है।
<curious>Definition याद करो: representative मतलब सिर्फ s-block या p-block, groups one, two, और thirteen to seventeen।</curious> Full configurations मत लिखो; बस हर एक को locate करो।
Atomic number twelve magnesium है - neon core, three s two। इसका last electron s subshell में है, तो ये s-block है, और इसलिए representative। यही हमारा answer है।
बाकी तीनों three d series में बैठते हैं। Twenty four chromium है, twenty six iron है, twenty nine copper है - हर एक d-block transition metal।
तो जवाब है atomic number twelve, magnesium।
Trap ध्यान दो: तीनों distractors transition metals हैं। जो student भूल जाता है कि representative elements d-block को exclude करते हैं, वो सीधे गलत choice की तरफ लुभा लिया जाएगा।
तो इसे crisp रखो: representative मतलब सिर्फ s या p। जिस पल आप कोई three d element देखो, वो दौड़ से बाहर है।

sections.subtopic: Electronic Configuration & the s, p, d, f Blocks
sections.title: Worked example: full placement for Z = 25

board_events.text: Worked Example: full placement for Z = 25
For $Z = 25$: write the configuration, then find period, block, group, and one block property.
Configuration: $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}$.
Period: highest n is 4. Block: last electron in 3d, so d-block.
Group: $(n-1)d + ns = 5 + 2 = 7$, so group 7.
Block property: as a transition metal it shows variable oxidation states, here from +2 up to +7.
This element is manganese - and it typically forms coloured compounds.
Configuration, d-block group rule, and a property

segments.text: Now a J E E Main question that asks for the full works - configuration, period, block, group, and a characteristic property - for the element with atomic number twenty five.
Start with the configuration. Building up to twenty five gives argon core, three d five, four s two.
That half-filled three d five is worth noticing, but here it arises naturally at manganese rather than as an anomaly.
<curious>Now read off period and block.</curious> The highest principal quantum number is four, so it is period four. The last electron went into the three d subshell, so it is a d-block element.
For the group, apply the d-block rule: the n minus one d electrons plus the n s electrons, which is five plus two, equals seven. So it is in group seven.
For a block property, being a transition metal it shows variable oxidation states - here running all the way from plus two up to plus seven, using both its three d and four s electrons.
And that identifies it: the element with atomic number twenty five is manganese, which characteristically forms coloured compounds.
So the chain is: configuration, then the d-block group rule, then a block-to-property inference. Three skills, one clean answer.
अब एक J E E Main question जो पूरा काम माँगता है - configuration, period, block, group, और एक characteristic property - atomic number twenty five वाले element के लिए।
Configuration से शुरू करो। Twenty five तक build करने पर मिलता है argon core, three d five, four s two।
वो half-filled three d five notice करने लायक है, पर यहाँ ये manganese पर naturally आता है, किसी anomaly के रूप में नहीं।
<curious>अब period और block पढ़ो।</curious> सबसे ऊँचा principal quantum number four है, तो ये period four है। Last electron three d subshell में गया, तो ये d-block element है।
Group के लिए, d-block rule लगाओ: n minus one d electrons plus n s electrons, जो five plus two, बराबर seven। तो ये group seven में है।
एक block property के लिए, transition metal होने से ये variable oxidation states दिखाता है - यहाँ plus two से लेकर plus seven तक, अपने three d और four s दोनों electrons इस्तेमाल करते हुए।
और ये इसे पहचान देता है: atomic number twenty five वाला element manganese है, जो characteristically coloured compounds बनाता है।
तो chain है: configuration, फिर d-block group rule, फिर block-to-property inference। तीन skills, एक साफ answer।

sections.subtopic: Electronic Configuration & the s, p, d, f Blocks
sections.title: Worked example: identify X with configuration [Ar]3d5 4s1

board_events.text: Worked Example: identify X with configuration [Ar]3d5 4s1
(a) Why does this differ from the naive Aufbau prediction?
Naive Aufbau predicts $[Ar]3d^{4}4s^{2}$; the actual $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ buys the stability of a half-filled $3d^{5}$.
The half-filled set is extra stable: symmetrical distribution, maximum exchange energy, minimum repulsion. This is chromium, $Z = 24$.
(b) Highest n is 4 - period 4; last electron in 3d - d-block; group = $5 + 1 = 6$.
(c) X is a transition element: the strict rule needs a partially filled d-subshell, and chromium's $3d^{5}$ qualifies.
Contrast zinc ($3d^{10}4s^{2}$): its d-subshell is full in the atom and in $Zn^{2+}$, so zinc is not a true transition metal.
Anomalous configuration, then place, then classify

segments.text: We close the worked examples - and the chapter's teaching - with a J E E Advanced question about an element X whose ground-state configuration is argon core, three d five, four s one.
Part a asks why this differs from what naive Aufbau would predict.

<whisper>Naive Aufbau would predict argon core, three d four, four s two.</whisper> The actual configuration, three d five, four s one, arises because a half-filled three d five subshell is extra stable, so one four s electron is promoted across to reach it.
That half-filled stability comes from a symmetrical electron distribution, maximum exchange energy, and minimum repulsion - and this identifies X as chromium, atomic number twenty four.

Part b, placement. The highest principal quantum number is four, so period four; the last electron is in three d, so d-block; and the group is n minus one d plus n s, which is five plus one, equals six.

Part c, classification. X is a transition element, because the strict definition requires a partially filled d-subshell in the atom or a stable ion - and chromium's three d five is partially filled, so it qualifies.

Contrast that with zinc, three d ten four s two. Zinc's d-subshell is completely full both in the atom and in the zinc two plus ion, so despite sitting in the d-block, zinc is not a true transition metal.
So the full workflow, one last time: spot the anomalous configuration and explain it, then place the element, then classify it against the strict definition. That is the complete Sub-four skill set.
हम worked examples - और chapter की teaching - को एक J E E Advanced question से बंद करते हैं, एक element X के बारे में जिसकी ground-state configuration argon core, three d five, four s one है।
Part a पूछता है कि ये naive Aufbau की prediction से अलग क्यों है।

<whisper>Naive Aufbau predict करता argon core, three d four, four s two।</whisper> Actual configuration, three d five, four s one, इसलिए आती है क्योंकि half-filled three d five subshell extra stable है, तो एक four s electron उस तक पहुँचने के लिए promote हो जाता है।
वो half-filled stability एक symmetrical electron distribution, maximum exchange energy, और minimum repulsion से आती है - और ये X को chromium, atomic number twenty four, के रूप में पहचान देती है।
Part b, placement। सबसे ऊँचा principal quantum number four है, तो period four; last electron three d में है, तो d-block; और group n minus one d plus n s, जो five plus one, बराबर six।

Part c, classification। X एक transition element है, क्योंकि strict definition atom या किसी stable ion में partially filled d-subshell माँगती है - और chromium का three d five partially filled है, तो ये qualify करता है।
इसके उलट zinc, three d ten four s two। Zinc का d-subshell atom में और zinc two plus ion दोनों में completely full है, तो d-block में बैठने के बावजूद, zinc true transition metal नहीं है।
तो पूरा workflow, आखिरी बार: anomalous configuration पकड़ो और explain करो, फिर element को place करो, फिर strict definition के खिलाफ classify करो। यही पूरा Sub-four skill set है।

sections.subtopic: Electronic Configuration & the s, p, d, f Blocks
sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Common pitfalls and pro-tips
Pitfall 1: reading the period from the wrong shell. Period = highest n, not the shell of the last d or f electron. For $[Ar]3d^{6}4s^{2}$, period is 4.
Pitfall 2: counting the d-block group wrong. Group = $(n-1)d + ns$ - you must add the ns electrons, not just count the d electrons.
Pitfall 3: calling every d-block element a transition metal. Strictly, Zn, Cd, Hg ($d^{10}$) are excluded.
Pitfall 4: treating He as s-block by configuration. Its $1s^{2}$ looks s-block, but it is placed in group 18 by property.
Pro-tip: for the block, jump straight to the last subshell filled - ignore everything before it.
For the group, use the quick map: s means count $ns$; p means 10 + (outer $s + p$); d means $(n-1)d + ns$.
Keep the staircase memorised - B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te - and reach for the Cr / Cu exception the moment either appears.

segments.text: Let's close Sub-four - and the chapter's teaching - with the traps and the shortcuts.

<whisper>Pitfall one: reading the period from the wrong shell.</whisper> The period is the highest principal quantum number in the configuration, not the shell of the last-filled d or f electron. For iron, argon core three d six four s two, the period is four - from the four s - not three.
Pitfall two: counting the d-block group wrong. The group is n minus one d plus n s - you must add the n s electrons, not just count the d electrons on their own.
Pitfall three: calling every d-block element a transition metal. Strictly, zinc, cadmium, and mercury, all d ten, are excluded from the true transition metals.
Pitfall four: treating helium as s-block from its bare configuration. One s two does look s-block, but helium is placed in group eighteen by property. Don't let the raw configuration mislead you.
Now the pro-tips. For any find-the-block question, jump straight to the last subshell filled and ignore everything before it - the block is decided there alone.
For the group, keep the quick map ready: s-block means count the n s electrons; p-block means ten plus the outer s and p; d-block means n minus one d plus n s.

And keep two things memorised cold: the metalloid staircase - boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium - and the chromium and copper exception, which you reach for the instant either element appears.
चलो Sub-four - और chapter की teaching - को traps और shortcuts से बंद करते हैं।

<whisper>Pitfall one: period को गलत shell से पढ़ना।</whisper> Period configuration में highest principal quantum number है, last-filled d या f electron का shell नहीं। Iron के लिए, argon core three d six four s two, period four है - four s से - three नहीं।
Pitfall two: d-block group गलत गिनना। Group n minus one d plus n s है - आपको n s electrons जोड़ने होते हैं, सिर्फ d electrons अकेले नहीं गिनने।
Pitfall three: हर d-block element को transition metal कहना। सख्ती से, zinc, cadmium, और mercury, सब d ten, true transition metals से बाहर हैं।
Pitfall four: helium को उसकी bare configuration से s-block मानना। One s two s-block जैसा दिखता ज़रूर है, पर helium property से group eighteen में रखा जाता है। Raw configuration को गुमराह मत करने दो।
अब pro-tips। किसी भी find-the-block question के लिए, सीधे last subshell filled पर jump करो और उससे पहले का सब कुछ ignore करो - block वहीं अकेले तय होता है।
Group के लिए, quick map तैयार रखो: s-block मतलब n s electrons गिनो; p-block मतलब ten plus outer s और p; d-block मतलब n minus one d plus n s।
और दो चीज़ें पक्की याद रखो: metalloid staircase - boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium - और chromium व copper exception, जिसकी तरफ आप उसी पल बढ़ते हो जब इनमें से कोई element दिखे।

segments.text: Before the final cheat sheet, let's gather every working relation from the whole chapter into one recap panel.
From Sub-one, the triad rule: the middle atomic mass is approximately the average of the first and last.
From Sub-two, the master engine: effective nuclear charge equals Z minus sigma - the heart of every physical trend.
Also from Sub-two, the size relations: the covalent radius is half the internuclear distance, and van der Waals is greater than metallic is greater than covalent.
The two energy definitions: ionisation, where a gaseous atom loses an electron with energy delta i H one; and electron gain, where a gaseous atom takes an electron with enthalpy delta e g H.

The three electronegativity scales: Mulliken as the average of ionisation energy and electron affinity, Pauling as roughly Mulliken over two point eight, and Allred-Rochow from Z effective over radius squared.
From Sub-three, valence for a representative element is N or eight minus N, and the maximum p-block oxidation state equals the total valence electrons.
And from Sub-four, the group rules: s-block is the n s count, p-block is ten plus the outer s and p, and d-block is n minus one d plus n s. That is the entire chapter's machinery on one board.
Final cheat sheet से पहले, चलो पूरे chapter की हर working relation को एक recap panel में इकट्ठा करते हैं।
Sub-one से, triad rule: middle atomic mass approximately first और last की average है।
Sub-two से, master engine: effective nuclear charge बराबर Z minus sigma - हर physical trend का दिल।
Sub-two से ही, size relations: covalent radius internuclear distance का आधा है, और van der Waals, metallic से बड़ा, जो covalent से बड़ा।
दो energy definitions: ionisation, जहाँ gaseous atom एक electron खोता है energy delta i H one के साथ; और electron gain, जहाँ gaseous atom एक electron लेता है enthalpy delta e g H के साथ।
तीन electronegativity scales: Mulliken ionisation energy और electron affinity की average के रूप में, Pauling करीब Mulliken बटा two point eight, और Allred-Rochow Z effective बटा radius squared से।
Sub-three से, एक representative element के लिए valence N या eight minus N है, और maximum p-block oxidation state total valence electrons के बराबर।
<excited>और Sub-four से, group rules: s-block n s count है, p-block ten plus outer s और p, और d-block n minus one d plus n s।</excited> यही पूरे chapter की machinery एक board पर।

board_events.text: Chapter cheat sheet
Laws: Mendeleev = periodic function of atomic weight; Modern (Moseley) = periodic function of atomic number Z.
Long form: 7 periods, 18 groups; period = highest n; recurrence numbers 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32. Naming Z greater than 100: nil-un-bi-tri-quad-pent-hex-sept-oct-enn, end in -ium.
Master arrow: across a period $Z_{\text{eff}}$ up, size down, IE up, EGE more negative, EN up. Down a group, all reverse.
Exception flags: Be greater than B and N greater than O (IE dips); Cl more negative than F (EGE); Ga smaller than Al (size and IE).
Chemical: reactivity peaks at both period ends; oxide Na2O basic to Al2O3 amphoteric to Cl2O7 acidic; diagonal pairs Li-Mg, Be-Al, B-Si.
Period-2 anomaly: no d-orbitals means no expanded octet - N max covalency 4, F only minus 1.
Blocks: s (1-2), p (13-18), d (3-12), f (below); strict transition needs a partially filled d, so Zn, Cd, Hg are excluded. Anomalies: Cr and Cu.

segments.text: And here is the one-screen cheat sheet for the entire chapter - the facts to have at your fingertips walking into the exam.
The two laws: Mendeleev's is a periodic function of atomic weight, and the modern law, Moseley's, is a periodic function of atomic number Z.

The long form: seven periods, eighteen groups, period equals the highest n, and the recurrence numbers two, eight, eight, eighteen, eighteen, thirty two, thirty two. For naming elements beyond atomic number one hundred, use the roots nil, un, bi, tri, quad, pent, hex, sept, oct, enn, ending in ium.

The physical master arrow: across a period, Z effective goes up, size goes down, ionisation enthalpy up, electron gain enthalpy more negative, and electronegativity up. Down a group, every one of those reverses.

The four exception flags: beryllium above boron and nitrogen above oxygen for the ionisation dips; chlorine more negative than fluorine for electron gain enthalpy; and gallium smaller than aluminium for size and ionisation energy.

The chemical trends: reactivity peaks at both ends of a period; oxides run from basic sodium oxide, through amphoteric aluminium oxide, to acidic dichlorine heptoxide; and the diagonal pairs are lithium-magnesium, beryllium-aluminium, and boron-silicon.
The period-two anomaly in one line: no d-orbitals means no expanded octet - nitrogen tops out at covalency four, and fluorine shows only minus one.

And the blocks: s is groups one and two, p is thirteen to eighteen, d is three to twelve, and f sits below; the strict transition definition needs a partially filled d, so zinc, cadmium, and mercury are excluded, and chromium and copper are the anomalous configurations. That is the whole chapter, ready to recall.
<curious>और ये रही पूरे chapter की one-screen cheat sheet - वो facts जो exam में जाते हुए उँगलियों पर होने चाहिए।</curious>
दो laws: Mendeleev की atomic weight का periodic function है, और modern law, Moseley की, atomic number Z का periodic function है।

Long form: सात periods, अठारह groups, period बराबर highest n, और recurrence numbers two, eight, eight, eighteen, eighteen, thirty two, thirty two। Atomic number एक सौ से आगे के elements name करने के लिए, roots इस्तेमाल करो nil, un, bi, tri, quad, pent, hex, sept, oct, enn, ium में खत्म।
Physical master arrow: period के across, Z effective ऊपर, size नीचे, ionisation enthalpy up, electron gain enthalpy ज़्यादा negative, और electronegativity up। Group में नीचे, इनमें से हर एक reverse।

चार exception flags: beryllium, boron के ऊपर और nitrogen, oxygen के ऊपर ionisation dips के लिए; chlorine, fluorine से ज़्यादा negative electron gain enthalpy के लिए; और gallium, aluminium से छोटा size और ionisation energy के लिए।

Chemical trends: reactivity period के दोनों सिरों पर peak करती है; oxides basic sodium oxide से, amphoteric aluminium oxide से होते हुए, acidic dichlorine heptoxide तक; और diagonal pairs हैं lithium-magnesium, beryllium-aluminium, और boron-silicon।
Period-two anomaly एक line में: कोई d-orbitals नहीं यानी कोई expanded octet नहीं - nitrogen covalency four पर रुकता है, और fluorine सिर्फ minus one दिखाता है।

और blocks: s groups one और two है, p thirteen to eighteen, d three to twelve, और f नीचे बैठता है; strict transition definition partially filled d माँगती है, तो zinc, cadmium, और mercury बाहर हैं, और chromium व copper anomalous configurations हैं। यही पूरा chapter, recall के लिए तैयार।
